actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Multi-Task Learning Approach to Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: Train a diffusion model as a shared prior on a joint task set of image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction. Use transfer learning to adapt the shared prior to each task, and sample from the learned posterior using a single set of hyperparameters. Implement a temperature schedule to control the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the sampling process.
CONTROLS: Use existing diffusion-based solvers DPS and DDRM as baselines, and ablate the temperature schedule to show its importance.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The shared prior can improve performance on each task, and the adaptive temperature schedule helps avoid spurious modes. However, poor task boundaries in the joint dataset could lead to reduced performance on individual tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: A Multi-Task Learning Approach to Inverse Problems (Revised)
PROPOSAL: (same as before) Train a diffusion model as a shared prior on a joint task set of image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction. Use transfer learning to adapt the shared prior to each task, and sample from the learned posterior using a single set of hyperparameters. Implement a temperature schedule to control the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the sampling process. Additionally, apply transfer learning in the reverse direction: freeze the task-specific adapter layers and fine-tune the shared prior on each task for a few epochs. This should allow the shared prior to specialize in each task without losing transfer knowledge.
CONTROLS: Keep the existing baseline and ablation, and add comparison to a model that transfers knowledge only from task-to-task, without reverse transfer.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The shared prior with reverse transfer can achieve better performance on each task, particularly in phase retrieval and HDR image reconstruction, while maintaining the benefits of transfer learning. However, the computational cost and potential overfitting could become issues for very large datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: A Multi-Task Learning Approach to Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: Train a diffusion model as a shared prior on a joint task set of image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction. Use transfer learning to adapt the shared prior to each task, and sample from the learned posterior using a single set of hyperparameters. Implement a temperature schedule to control the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the sampling process. Additionally, apply transfer learning in the reverse direction: freeze the task-specific adapter layers and fine-tune the shared prior on each task for a few epochs. This should allow the shared prior to specialize in each task without losing transfer knowledge.
CONTROLS: DPS and DDRM as baselines, a ablation study on the fully connected layers as ice point of stabilization in tail.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The shared prior with reverse transfer can achieve better performance on each task, particularly in phase retrieval and HDR image reconstruction, while maintaining the benefits of transfer learning. However, the computational cost and potential overfitting could become issues for very large datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Denoising Strategies for Handling Unknown Noise Levels
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of the diffusion model on inverse problems with unknown noise levels by using different denoising strategies, such as reducing the strength of the denoising noise, and adaptively selecting the noise level based on the restored image's entropy. Evaluate the performance of these strategies on the HDR image reconstruction and phase retrieval tasks, which are particularly sensitive to noise.
CONTROLS: Use the same setup as proposal 1, and add baseline comparisons with existing methods that use hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping to handle unknown noise levels.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The diffusion model with adaptively selected noise level can provide the best performance on both HDR image reconstruction and phase retrieval tasks, but may require additional calibration for each task. Reducing the strength of the denoising noise may lead to improved results on phase retrieval, but might not generalize well to other tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Control in Diffusion-Based Solvers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of the temperature schedule on exploration-exploitation control in the diffusion-based solver, and develop a novel algorithm that can dynamically adjust the temperature based on the uncertainty of the estimated posterior distribution. This should allow the solver to adapt to the complexity of the inverse problem and provide better reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed algorithm with existing diffusion-based solvers, including DPIR and DDRM, and evaluate its performance on various noise levels and inverse problems.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm can provide better reconstructions on various inverse problems, particularly in cases where the noise level is unknown or the posterior distribution is highly uncertain. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probabilistic Initialization for Improved Sampling Efficiency
PROPOSAL: Examine the effect of probabilistic initialization on the sampling efficiency of the diffusion-based solver, and propose a new initialization strategy based on the unknown data distribution. Specifically, use a probabilistic neural network to estimate the data distribution and sample from it to initialize the solver. This should lead to more efficient sampling and better reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed initialization strategy with existing methods, such as uniform or normal initialization, and evaluate its performance on various inverse problems and noise levels.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The probabilistic initialization strategy can significantly improve the sampling efficiency of the diffusion-based solver, especially in cases where the data distribution is complex or unknown. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and a large enough dataset for the probabilistic neural network to converge.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Denoising Strategies for Handling Unknown Noise Levels
PROPOSAL: Investigation of denoising strategies can be combined with the sampling efficiency improvement of probabilistic initialization. Introduce a probabilistic prior for the denoising process, allowing the model to automatically adjust its denoising strength based on the estimated data distribution. This can lead to even better reconstructions and improved handling of unknown noise levels.
CONTROLS: Use the same set of baseline comparisons as before, but now also include a comparison with the revised probabilistic initialization method from proposal 4. Also, experiment with various distribution families for the probabilistic prior and analyze its impact on the performance.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The combination of denoising strategies and probabilistic initiation should bring further improvements in handling unknown noise levels and can provide more robust reconstructions even when the data distribution is complex or unknown.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Phase Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Address the problem of phase retrieval in the context of inverse problems by introducing an adversary that aims to make the original signal indistinguishable from its reconstruction. Use a combination of denoising and adversarial training to develop a phase-unaware reconstruction that can handle missing phase information in the measurements. Evaluate the performance on various phase retrieval scenarios and compare it with baseline methods.
CONTROLS: Use existing phase retrieval methods as baselines, such as iterative hard thresholding and diffrane-GAUSS-SENSE. Evaluate the performance on synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adversarial training approach can significantly improve the phase retrieval accuracy by forcing the model to learn a phase-aware representation of the signal. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and a large enough dataset for effective training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Automated Hyperparameter Tuning
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to automate the hyperparameter tuning process for the diffusion-based inverse problem solver. Each agent will focus on a specific hyperparameter, and the agents will interact and learn from each other to find the optimal set of hyperparameters for the task at hand. Evaluate the performance on various inverse problems and compare it with baseline hyperparameter tuning methods.
CONTROLS: Use existing hyperparameter tuning methods, such as grid search and random search, as baselines. Evaluate the performance on synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-agent reinforcement learning framework can significantly speed up the hyperparameter tuning process and improve the performance of the inverse problem solver on various tasks. However, it may require careful tuning of the agent architectures and hyperparameters, and large-scale computing resources for effective training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Inference Framework for Diffusion-Based Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified inference framework that combines the diffusion-based solver with the various techniques and methods proposed in the previous experiments (multi-task learning, denoising strategies, probabilistic initialization, adversarial training, and multi-agent reinforcement learning). This unified framework should provide a robust and efficient solution for a wide range of inverse problems, including image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and HDR image reconstruction. Evaluate the performance on various inverse problems and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Use the existing experimental setup and comparisons to validate the performance of the unified inference framework.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified inference framework can significantly improve the state-of-the-art performance on various inverse problems by leveraging the strengths of each individual technique and method. However, it may require careful tuning of the overall framework architecture and hyperparameters, and large-scale computing resources for effective training.

Develop a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to automate the hyperparameter tuning process for the diffusion-based inverse problem solver. Develop a unified inference framework that combines the diffusion-based solver with the various techniques and methods proposed in the previous experiments (multi-task learning, denoising strategies, probabilistic initialization, adversarial training, and multi-agent reinforcement learning). actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Diffusion Primer for Robust Inverse Problem Solving
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a new diffusion model-based solver for inverse problems, DIPS (Diffusion Inverse Problem Solver), which leverages a pretrained denoiser to generate manifold-adjacent perturbations of the input measurement that promote exploration of the solution space while maintaining feasibility on the data manifold. DIPS will utilize a learnable noise schedule adapted to the specific inverse problem, allowing it to adjust the exploration-exploitation trade-off based on the noise level and task difficulty.
CONTROLS: We will compare DIPS to existing diffusion-based solvers (e.g. DPS, DDRM) and deterministic MAP methods (e.g. DMPlug) on a suite of real-world benchmarks in image super-resolution, inpainting, deblurring, and phase retrieval.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DIPS will showcase robust performance across a range of noise levels and task difficulties, outperforming existing diffusion-based solvers and MAP methods in terms of fidelity, mode coverage, and noise robustness, but may struggle with severely ill-posed problems where the solution space is highly multimodal and the noise level is unknown.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Sampling with L2-Constrained Denoiser Feedback
PROPOSAL: We propose to design a novel denoiser feedback mechanism for DIPS, dubbed L2-DF, which constrains the perturbations to be L2-norm bounded. This will guarantee that the intermediate states produced by the denoiser remain close to the data manifold and enforce stability in the exploration process, reducing the risk of drifting off the learned manifold. We will also adapt the perturbation schedule to optimize the exploration-exploitation trade-off using a lower-bound of the L2-norm radius of the learnable noise schedule.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate L2-DF against a baseline using DIPS without L2-constrained denoiser feedback, and compare the results to existing diffusion-based solvers with likelihood-gradient corrections (e.g. DDRM, DPS).
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: L2-DF will significantly improve the robustness and fidelity of DIPS reconstructions, reducing the artifacts and overfitting to noise, but may limit the exploration of the solution space if the constraints are too tight.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Sampling with L2-Constrained Denoiser Feedback
PROPOSAL: We propose to enhance the L2-DF mechanism by incorporating a probabilistic variant that uses a mixture of Gaussian distributions to model the intermediate states. This will allow DIPS to adaptively adjust the L2-norm radius of the perturbations and balance exploration and exploitation in a data-dependent manner.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the probabilistic L2-DF against the deterministic L2-DF and the baseline DIPS without the L2-constrained denoiser feedback, as well as compare the results to existing diffusion-based solvers with spatial and temporal variance control (e.g. ΠGDM, TMPD).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The probabilistic L2-DF will significantly improve the robustness, flexibility, and adaptability of DIPS, enabling more robust reconstructions in complex scenarios with variable noise levels and task difficulties. However, it may introduce increased computational cost and require more careful tuning of the Gaussian mixture parameters.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Hierarchical Diffusion for Multi-Modal Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend DIPS with a hierarchical diffusion framework that captures the multi-modal nature of severely ill-posed inverse problems. This will consist of a multi-scale diffusion process, where each layer corresponds to a specific solution space, and a mixture-of-experts approach to combine the explorations from each layer. We will adapt the denoiser and perturbation schedules to the hierarchical framework to ensure stability and feasibility.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the hierarchical DIPS against a baseline using DIPS without hierarchical diffusion, as well as compare the results to existing methods for solving multi-modal inverse problems (e.g. ReSample, DiffPIR).
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical DIPS will demonstrate improved robustness, mode coverage, and accuracy in solving severely ill-posed inverse problems with multiple local modes, but may require careful tuning of the mixture-of-experts parameters and may exhibit higher computational cost due to the additional layers.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Measurement Noise Learning with Inverse Huber Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose to integrate an inverse Huber loss function into the learning process of DIPS to robustly estimate the measurement noise level from the data. This will enable DIPS to adapt to unknown measurement noise levels and task difficulties, reducing the need for hyperparameter tuning and early stopping. We will evaluate the robustness of the inverse Huber loss by comparing its estimates to the true noise levels.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the inverse Huber loss against a baseline using DIPS without noise learning, and compare the results to existing methods for noise estimation (e.g. noise estimation using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR)).
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The inverse Huber loss will demonstrate improved robustness, adaptability, and noise estimation accuracy of DIPS, but may require careful tuning of the Huber loss parameter and may exhibit increased computational cost due to the additional training process.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Inverse Problems with Pretrained Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage transfer learning to adapt pretrained diffusion models (e.g. DALL-E, StyleGAN) to new inverse problems. This will enable rapid deployment and adaptation of DIPS to novel tasks and domains, reducing the need for extensive training from scratch. We will evaluate the transferability and generality of the pretrained models on a range of inverse problems.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the transfer learning experiments against a baseline using DIPS trained from scratch, as well as compare the results to existing transfer learning methods for inverse problems (e.g. transfer learning using+SITCOM).
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach will demonstrate improved efficiency, rapid deployment, and flexibility of DIPS on a range of inverse problems, but may exhibit reduced performance on tasks with significantly different distributions or noise characteristics.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Inverse Problems with Pretrained Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to enhance the transfer learning approach by incorporating a noise adaptation module that adjusts the noise estimate and schedule for each target task based on the characteristics of the source task. This will help to reduce the gap between the source and target tasks, improving the effectiveness of the transfer learning. We will evaluate the impact of the noise adaptation module on the performance of DIPS.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the noise adaptation module against a baseline using the original transfer learning approach, and compare the results to existing transfer learning methods with noise adaptation (e.g. noise adaptation using ReSample).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The noise adaptation module will significantly improve the transferability and adaptability of DIPS, enabling more accurate and robust reconstructions on a range of inverse problems, but may require careful tuning of the noise adaptation parameters and may exhibit increased computational cost due to the additional training process.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Efficient Inverse Problem Solving with Multi-Scale Denoising Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a novel multi-scale denoising diffusion model architecture that hierarchically refines the estimation of the inverse problem solution. This will enable DIPS to efficiently leverage the power of denoising diffusion models on a range of inverse problems, from simple to complex, while reducing the computational cost and increasing the speed of convergence.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the multi-scale denoising diffusion model against a baseline using the standard denoising diffusion model architecture, as well as compare the results to existing methods for efficient inverse problem solving (e.g. multi-level solvers).
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-scale denoising diffusion model will demonstrate improved efficiency, speed of convergence, and robustness of DIPS, but may require careful tuning of the scale factors and may exhibit reduced performance on tasks with significantly different distributions or noise characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Bayesian Calibration of Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a Bayesian calibration framework for diffusion models that integrates uncertainty quantification of the diffusion process and the estimation of the inverse problem solution. This will enable DIPS to provide probabilistic uncertainty estimates of the reconstruction, which can be used for model selection, error estimation, and decision-making.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the Bayesian calibration framework against a baseline using standard diffusion model-based estimation, as well as compare the results to existing methods for Bayesian calibration of diffusion models (e.g. Bayesian optimization).
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Bayesian calibration framework will demonstrate improved uncertainty quantification, robustness, and interpretability of DIPS, but may require careful tuning of the calibration hyperparameters and may exhibit increased computational cost due to the integration of uncertainty quantification.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Real-World Benchmarking and Evaluation Framework for Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a comprehensive real-world benchmarking and evaluation framework for inverse problems that incorporates a range of state-of-the-art datasets and metrics from various domains, including computer vision, medical imaging, and signal processing. This will enable a rigorous and systematic evaluation of DIPS and other inverse problem solvers, facilitating comparison and innovation in the field.
CONTROLS: We will create a curated dataset and evaluation framework that includes real-world datasets, metrics, and baselines, such as PSNR, SSIM, and visually inspected metrics, to facilitate benchmarking and evaluation of DIPS.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation framework will enable a standardized and fair comparison of DIPS with other inverse problem solvers, facilitating the advancement of the field and improved reproducibility and transparency, but may require ongoing curation and updating of the dataset and evaluation metrics.

propositions.prediction: The multi-scale denoising diffusion model will demonstrate improved efficiency, speed of convergence, and robustness of DIPS, but may require careful tuning of the scale factors and may exhibit reduced performance on tasks with significantly different distributions or noise characteristics.
propositions.texte: We propose to develop a novel multi-scale denoising diffusion model architecture that hierarchically refines the estimation of the inverse problem solution. This will enable DIPS to efficiently leverage the power of denoising diffusion models on a range of inverse problems, from simple to complex, while reducing the computational cost and increasing the speed of convergence.
propositions.titre: Efficient Inverse Problem Solving with Multi-Scale Denoising Diffusion Models

propositions.controles: We will evaluate the performance of the Bayesian calibration framework against a baseline using standard diffusion model-based estimation, as well as compare the results to existing methods for Bayesian calibration of diffusion models (e.g. Bayesian optimization).
propositions.prediction: The Bayesian calibration framework will demonstrate improved uncertainty quantification, robustness, and interpretability of DIPS, but may require careful tuning of the calibration hyperparameters and may exhibit increased computational cost due to the integration of uncertainty quantification.
propositions.texte: We propose to develop a Bayesian calibration framework for diffusion models that integrates uncertainty quantification of the diffusion process and the estimation of the inverse problem solution. This will enable DIPS to provide probabilistic uncertainty estimates of the reconstruction, which can be used for model selection, error estimation, and decision-making.
propositions.titre: Bayesian Calibration of Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems

propositions.controles: We will create a curated dataset and evaluation framework that includes real-world datasets, metrics, and baselines, such as PSNR, SSIM, and visually inspected metrics, to facilitate benchmarking and evaluation of DIPS.
propositions.prediction: The evaluation framework will enable a standardized and fair comparison of DIPS with other inverse problem solvers, facilitating the advancement of the field and improved reproducibility and transparency, but may require ongoing curation and updating of the dataset and evaluation metrics.
propositions.texte: We propose to develop a comprehensive real-world benchmarking and evaluation framework for inverse problems that incorporates a range of state-of-the-art datasets and metrics from various domains, including computer vision, medical imaging, and signal processing. This will enable a rigorous and systematic evaluation of DIPS and other inverse problem solvers, facilitating comparison and innovation in the field.
propositions.titre: Real-World Benchmarking and Evaluation Framework for Inverse Problems

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Alignment-based Methods to Spurious Correlations
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a series of experiments on three real-world datasets in the digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification domains to investigate the robustness of three state-of-the-art alignment-based UDA methods (Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN), Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and Correlation Alignment (CORAL)) to spurious correlations.
CONTROLS: We will compare these methods to a baseline method that uses only labeled source data, and also evaluate the performance of these methods with and without debiasing techniques.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the alignment-based methods to generally perform worse on the target domain when spurious correlations are present in the source domain, and that debiasing techniques can improve performance by reducing the reliance on these shortcuts. However, these methods may still struggle with complex spurious correlations, and their performance may degrade significantly when the target data are scarce or imbalanced.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Label Noise on Pseudo-Labeling-based Methods
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how different types and amounts of label noise in the target domain affect the performance of three pseudo-labeling-based UDA methods (Entropy-based Pseudo-Labeling, Self-Training with Target-domain-Adversarial Training, and Joint Parallel Self-Training).
CONTROLS: We will add noise to the target labels and compare the performance of these methods to the noise-free baseline, as well as to the alignment-based methods from our previous experiment.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that increased label noise will lead to more aggressive pseudo-labeling, where the model over-confidently predicts labels that are unrelated to their true values, causing the model to diverge from its optimal solution. Furthermore, we anticipate that pseudo-labeling-based methods will perform worse than alignment-based methods in the presence of label noise, especially when the target data are scarce or imbalanced.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Limitations of Group Distributionally Robust Optimization
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the limitations of group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) methods in the context of UDA, particularly when the source data contain spurious correlations and the target data are scarce or imbalanced.
CONTROLS: We will compare GDRO methods to existing UDA baselines and evaluate their performance on datasets in the digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification domains.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect GDRO methods to perform well when the target data are abundant and the source data are clean, but to struggle with complex spurious correlations and data scarcity, similar to other UDA methods. Furthermore, we anticipate that GDRO methods will require significant computational resources to achieve good performance, which may be impractical for large-scale UDA tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Use of Counterfactual Learning for UDA
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of counterfactual learning (CFL) for UDA, which involves learning a model that can predict the target labels by conditioning on counterfactual versions of the source data.
CONTROLS: We will compare CFL-based methods to existing UDA baselines and evaluate their performance on datasets in the digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification domains.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CFL-based methods to perform well when the source and target distributions are related in a complex way, but may struggle with datasets where the relationships are not well-captured by counterfactual versions. Additionally, we anticipate that CFL-based methods will require significant expertise to design effective counterfactual versions of the source data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Alignment-based Methods to Spurious Correlations
PROPOSAL: We will add more depth to experiment 1 by using feature importance analysis to diagnose the features that alignment-based methods are relying on when the target domain is significantly different from the source domain, and how the performance improves when those features are removed or debiased.
CONTROLS: We will compare the feature importance results to the original alignment-based methods and evaluate the performance of these methods with and without debiasing techniques.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the alignment-based methods to perform worse in the presence of spurious correlations, and that the feature importance analysis will reveal which features are most responsible for this degradation in performance. Furthermore, we anticipate that debiasing techniques can help mitigate this issue, but may not completely eliminate it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Pseudo-Labeling-based Methods with Bootstrapped Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: We will modify pseudo-labeling-based methods to use bootstrapped uncertainty estimates, which improve the robustness of the pseudo-labels by leveraging multiple samples to estimate the predictions' uncertainty.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of bootstrapped uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling to existing pseudo-labeling baselines and evaluate their performance on datasets in the digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification domains.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect bootstrapped uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling to perform better than existing pseudo-labeling methods in the presence of label noise or data scarcity, as it can provide more accurate estimates of uncertainty. However, we anticipate that bootstrapping may also introduce additional computational overhead, which could be a limitation in large-scale UDA tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Multi-Task Learning for UDA
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of multi-task learning for UDA, where a single model is trained on multiple tasks simultaneously, including the primary task of classification and secondary tasks that provide information about the target domain, such as image segmentation or object detection.
CONTROLS: We will compare multi-task learning-based methods to existing UDA baselines and evaluate their performance on datasets in the digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification domains.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning-based methods to perform better than existing UDA methods by leveraging additional information from secondary tasks, but may struggle with datasets where the relationships between tasks are complex orWhere the tasks are not informative.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Novel Dataset for Simulated Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel synthetic dataset that mimics real-world distribution shift scenarios, allowing for a controlled investigation of the robustness of UDA methods under different distribution shift types and severity levels.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of UDA methods on our novel dataset to existing UDA baselines and evaluate their performance under different distribution shift types and severity levels.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our novel dataset to provide valuable insights into the robustness of UDA methods and help identify which methods are more suitable for real-world distribution shift scenarios. However, we anticipate that training and validation may require significant computational resources, and that the synthetic nature of the dataset may limit its direct generalizability to real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Integrating UDA Methods for Improved Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of integrating multiple UDA methods to improve generalization performance on target domains with significant distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of different combinations of UDA methods (e.g., alignment, pseudo-labeling, multi-task learning) to existing baselines and evaluate their performance on our novel synthetic dataset and real-world datasets.
COST: 420 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that integrating multiple UDA methods can lead to improved generalization performance, but also anticipate potential challenges in combining different methods and selecting the most effective combination for a given dataset.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Target-Prior Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Iterative Refining
PROPOSAL: We design an iterative algorithm that simultaneously adapts feature representation, aligns source and target distributions, and improves pseudo-label quality through an adaptive target-prior. Specifically, we first initialize a feature embedding space by training a network on the source domain. Then, we employ a recent alignment method to reduce the discrepancy between the source and target domains and calculate a new target-prior from the target pseudo-labels. We develop a novel pseudo-label refinement strategy that adjusts the confidence of each target pseudo-label based on the similarity between the source and target distributions. This updated target-prior is then combined with the source labels to fine-tune the feature embedding network. We iterate this refinement process, adapting feature representations, distributions, and target priors until convergence.
CONTROLS: We compare to recent alignment methods, such as MMD and CORAL, and pseudo-labeling methods, such as Entropy Min and LSCP, and also a baseline model without adaptation. We also ablate the effect of the number of iterations, pseudo-label refinement strategy, and the choice of feature embedding network.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our algorithm is expected to outperform state-of-the-art alignment and pseudo-labeling methods due to the synergistic benefits of iterative refinement of both feature representation and target distribution. However, performance might degrade if the source and target domains exhibit extremely different characteristics that cannot be effectively captured by a fixed feature space.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Distributionally Robust Domain Adaptation with Group-Cluster Wasserstein Bounding
PROPOSAL: We propose a new distributionally robust domain adaptation framework, termed Group-Cluster Wasserstein Bounding (GCWB), which leverages the strengths of distributionally robust optimization and group-based domain adaptation. Specifically, we introduce a group-cluster structure to the target domain and derive an upper bound on the target risk using a Wasserstein distance between the source and target distributions. We then minimize this upper bound over the source domain, obtaining a risk tolerance that reflects the uncertainty due to domain shift. This allows us to adapt to bothgroup-structured and complex domain shifts without relying on strong assumptions about the group labels or explicit estimation of the target distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare GCWB to state-of-the-art alignment and distributionally robust optimization methods, such as Group DRO, and also evaluate the effect of using different group-cluster structures and the sensitivity to the choice of risk tolerance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GCWB is expected to outperform existing approaches on group-structured domain shifts, particularly when the number of groups is relatively small. However, performance might decrease when the group structure is complex or when the target domain is severely imbalanced.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Distributionally Robust Domain Adaptation with Group-Cluster Wasserstein Bounding
PROPOSAL: We modify the GCWB approach to incorporate a self-training component that iteratively refines the group assignments and the target pseudo-labels. Specifically, we first adapt the feature representation to the source domain using the group-cluster structure and obtain a risk tolerance based on the Wasserstein distance. Then, we refine the group assignments and the target pseudo-labels using a clustering-based approach that leverages both the source labels and the target features. We update the risk tolerance and the feature representation based on the refined group assignments and pseudo-labels, and iterate this process until convergence.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised GCWB to the original GCWB and other self-training methods, such as Pseudo-Label and Entropy Min, and also evaluate the effect of using different clustering algorithms and the sensitivity to the choice of self-training iterations.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised GCWB is expected to improve performance on complex domain shifts and subgroup-structured shifts, particularly when the target domain is severely imbalanced. However, performance might degrade if the source domain is complex or if the group assignments are inaccurate.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Domain Adaptation via Causal Graph Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose a weakly-supervised domain adaptation framework that infers a causal graph from the source domain and then uses it to adapt to the target domain. The causal graph encodes the underlying dependencies between features and captures the causal relationships that are invariant across domains. We use a recent causal graph inference algorithm to learn the graph structure from the source domain, and then use it to identify the causal features that are relevant to the task and adapt the target feature representation to align with the causal graph.
CONTROLS: We compare to recent weakly-supervised domain adaptation methods, such as WEAp and CAFFE, and also evaluate the effect of using different causal graph inference algorithms and the sensitivity to the choice of causal features.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach is expected to outperform existing weakly-supervised domain adaptation methods on tasks with complex causal relationships, particularly when the source domain is rich in features and the target domain is sparse. However, performance might degrade if the causal graph inference algorithm is unreliable or if the causal features are difficult to identify.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Exploring the Role of Adversarial Training in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effectiveness of adversarial training in unsupervised domain adaptation, where the generator aims to deceive the discriminator into classifying samples as from the target domain. We propose to use a self-supervised adversarial training framework that combines domain-invariant feature learning with adversarial training. Specifically, we first learn a domain-invariant feature space using a recent alignment method, and then add an adversarial training component that uses a discriminator to distinguish between source and target domain samples.
CONTROLS: We compare to recent adversarial training methods, such as DANN and CDAN, and also evaluate the effect of using different alignment methods and the sensitivity to the choice of adversarial loss.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our self-supervised adversarial training framework is expected to improve performance on tasks with minor domain shifts, particularly when the source domain is small and the target domain is large. However, performance might degrade if the domain shift is severe or if the discriminator is unreliable.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Target-Prior Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Iterative Refining
PROPOSAL: We modify the initial framework to incorporate the weakly-supervised component of our recent causal graph inference work. Specifically, we use the causal graph learned from the source domain to refine the target-prior and improve the pseudo-label quality. We adapt the feature representation to align with the causal graph, and then use the refined target-prior to improve the feature representation and the pseudo-label quality in an iterative manner. We evaluate the performance on tasks where the target domain is severely imbalanced and the causal relationships are complex.
CONTROLS: We compare to the original Target-Prior framework and the revised Group-Cluster Wasserstein Bounding framework, and also evaluate the effect of using different causal graph inference algorithms and the sensitivity to the choice of target-prior refinement iterations.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised Target-Prior framework is expected to outperform the original version on tasks with complex causal relationships and severe domain shifts, particularly when the target domain is imbalanced. However, performance might degrade if the causal graph inference algorithm is unreliable or if the target-prior refinement iterations are insufficient.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning framework for unsupervised domain adaptation, where the model learns to adapt to different domains and tasks in a meta-learning setting. Specifically, we first train a set of meta-learners on different source-domain-target-domain pairs, each representing a different adaptation task. Then, we use a meta-controller to select the most relevant meta-learner for a given target domain and fine-tune it for the new task. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Examining the Impact of Labeled Source Data Quantity on Adversarial Domain Adaptation Performance
PROPOSAL: Train a source-only classifier using the Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) method on a dataset from a source domain, and then evaluate its performance on both the target domain and a randomly shuffled version of the target domain to simulate real-world distribution shifts. We compare the performance under different amounts of labeled source data, from a small to a large set.
CONTROLS: Source-only ERM on the target domain serves as our baseline, and we compare against pseudo-labeling methods and state-of-the-art adaptation approaches that do explicit domain alignment.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With limited source data, performance on the target domain is more vulnerable to distribution shifts than when source data is abundant, leading to a trade-off between adapter performance and robustness to distribution shifts that depends on the characteristics of the source and target data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Domain-Invariant Feature Learning under Spurious Correlations
PROPOSAL: Train domain-invariant feature learning models on synthetic datasets where the feature correlations are artificially introduced to mimic real-world spurious correlations, such as background or color in image classification. We evaluate the models' ability to correctly disentangle the true task-relevant features from the spurious ones and assess how this ability is impacted under different strengths of spurious correlations.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against the baselines of general-purpose feature extractors (e.g., ResNet) and explore the relationship between the performance of domain-invariant feature learning and the strength of spurious correlations.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that domain-invariant feature learning models can to some extent mitigate the negative impact of spurious correlations, but strong correlations might still lead to poor disentanglement results, suggesting a need for robust and adaptive methods that can adapt to varying task characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Learning from Limited Target Data: Effect of Unlabeled Target Data Quantity on Adaptation Performance
PROPOSAL: Compare the adaptation performance of the baseline ERM method and a pseudo-labeling method on the MNIST dataset under different amounts of labeled source data and unlabeled target data. We test adaptation performance in both the digit recognition and facial attribute classification tasks.
CONTROLS: ERM on labeled target data serves as our baseline, and we compare against state-of-the-art methods that leverage unlabeled target data.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that pseudo-labeling can provide a boost in adaptation performance when large amounts of unlabeled target data are available, but this effect diminishes with decreasing target data quantities, suggesting a trade-off between the amount of available target data and adaptation performance.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Learning from Limited Target Data: Effect of Unlabeled Target Data Quantity on Adaptation Performance (Revision 1)
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous proposal to explore the effect of unlabeled target data quantity on adaptation performance in the bird image classification task using the CUB-200-2011 dataset. In addition to comparing the adaptation performance of the baseline ERM method and a pseudo-labeling method under different amounts of labeled source data and unlabeled target data, we also investigate the impact of the data imbalance between the source and target domains on adaptation performance.
CONTROLS: ERM on labeled target data serves as our baseline, and we compare against state-of-the-art methods that leverage unlabeled target data and handle data imbalance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that pseudo-labeling can provide a boost in adaptation performance even when the target data is imbalanced and scarce, but the improvement may come at the cost of overfitting to the majority class in the target domain.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Learning from Limited Target Data: Effect of Unlabeled Target Data Quantity on Adaptation Performance
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous proposal to include a counterfactual explanation mechanism to investigate the impact of feature importance under spurious correlations.
CONTROLS: To validate our results, we will compare against the original pseudo-labeling method without the counterfactual explanation mechanism and explore the effect of varying the percentage of input features used for the counterfactual explanation on adaptation performance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing the feature importance under spurious correlations, we expect that our modified pseudo-labeling method can better disentangle task-relevant features from task-irrelevant ones and provide improved adaptation performance, especially in scenarios with limited target data and data imbalance between the source and target domains.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Robust Distributionally Robust Optimization for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose to modify the standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO) method to handle unsupervised domain adaptation by using a learnable ambiguity set that adapts to the distribution of the target data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art DRO methods and UDA methods that do not use DRO.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By learning a more accurate representation of the target data distribution, we expect that our proposed method can provide superior performance and robustness against distribution shifts in the target domain, especially in scenarios with limited target data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Augmenting Unlabeled Target Data with Adversarial Training for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose to augment the unlabeled target data by applying adversarial perturbations to the input data, which helps to increase the robustness and diversity of the target data for unsupervised domain adaptation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art UDA methods that do not use adversarial training, as well as our own method without the augmentation step.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By augmenting the unlabeled target data with adversarial training, we expect that our proposed method can improve the quality and diversity of the target data, leading to better adaptation performance, especially in scenarios with limited target data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Transferability of Pre-Trained Features for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation on Different Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the transferability of pre-trained features, such as those obtained from ImageNet, on different domains, including digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification, to assess their adaptability to new tasks and domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare the transferability of different pre-trained models, such as ResNet and Vgg, and explore the impact of fine-tuning on the performance of transfer learning in UDA settings.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that certain pre-trained features, such as those obtained from ImageNet, will demonstrate good transferability across domains, but the effectiveness of transfer learning will depend on the target task and domain, as well as the quality of the pre-training data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Error-Correcting Codes for Robust Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose to use error-correcting codes, inspired by techniques from coding theory, to construct a robust adaptation framework for unsupervised domain adaptation, by encoding the input target data and generating predictions that are robust against noise and corruption.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art UDA methods and explore the impact of different error-correcting codes and noise levels on the robustness of the adaptation framework.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating error-correcting codes into our adaptation framework will enable us to achieve robust and highly accurate predictions on the target domain, even when the input data is noisy or corrupted.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Multi-Task Learning with Self-Supervised Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework that combines self-supervised representation learning and supervised domain adaptation to align the feature distributions of the source and target domains.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method on several benchmark datasets and compare it against state-of-the-art UDA methods.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging self-supervised representation learning and multi-task learning, we expect that our proposed method can align the feature distributions across domains and achieve state-of-the-art performance on several unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.

propositions.texte: Train domain-invariant feature learning models on synthetic datasets where the feature correlations are artificially introduced to mimic real-world spurious correlations, such as background or color in image classification. We evaluate the models' ability to correctly disentangle the true task-relevant features from the spurious ones and assess how this ability is impacted under different strengths of spurious correlations.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Effectiveness of Domain-Invariant Feature Learning under Spurious Correlations

propositions.controles: ERM on labeled target data serves as our baseline, and we compare against state-of-the-art methods that leverage unlabeled target data.
propositions.prediction: We anticipate that pseudo-labeling can provide a boost in adaptation performance when large amounts of unlabeled target data are available, but this effect diminishes with decreasing target data quantities, suggesting a trade-off between the amount of available target data and adaptation performance.
propositions.texte: Compare the adaptation performance of the baseline ERM method and a pseudo-labeling method on the MNIST dataset under different amounts of labeled source data and unlabeled target data. We test adaptation performance in both the digit recognition and facial attribute classification tasks.
propositions.titre: Learning from Limited Target Data: Effect of Unlabeled Target Data Quantity on Adaptation Performance

propositions.controles: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art DRO methods and UDA methods that do not use DRO.
propositions.prediction: By learning a more accurate representation of the target data distribution, we expect that our proposed method can provide superior performance and robustness against distribution shifts in the target domain, especially in scenarios with limited target data.
propositions.texte: We propose to modify the standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO) method to handle unsupervised domain adaptation by using a learnable ambiguity set that adapts to the distribution of the target data.
propositions.titre: Robust Distributionally Robust Optimization for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

propositions.controles: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art UDA methods that do not use adversarial training, as well as our own method without the augmentation step.
propositions.prediction: By augmenting the unlabeled target data with adversarial training, we expect that our proposed method can improve the quality and diversity of the target data, leading to better adaptation performance, especially in scenarios with limited target data.
propositions.texte: We propose to augment the unlabeled target data by applying adversarial perturbations to the input data, which helps to increase the robustness and diversity of the target data for unsupervised domain adaptation.
propositions.titre: Augmenting Unlabeled Target Data with Adversarial Training for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

propositions.controles: We will compare the transferability of different pre-trained models, such as ResNet and Vgg, and explore the impact of fine-tuning on the performance of transfer learning in UDA settings.
propositions.prediction: We expect that certain pre-trained features, such as those obtained from ImageNet, will demonstrate good transferability across domains, but the effectiveness of transfer learning will depend on the target task and domain, as well as the quality of the pre-training data.
propositions.texte: We evaluate the transferability of pre-trained features, such as those obtained from ImageNet, on different domains, including digit recognition, facial attribute classification, and bird image classification, to assess their adaptability to new tasks and domains.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Transferability of Pre-Trained Features for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation on Different Domains

propositions.controles: We will compare our proposed method against state-of-the-art UDA methods and explore the impact of different error-correcting codes and noise levels on the robustness of the adaptation framework.
propositions.prediction: We expect that incorporating error-correcting codes into our adaptation framework will enable us to achieve robust and highly accurate predictions on the target domain, even when the input data is noisy or corrupted.
propositions.texte: We propose to use error-correcting codes, inspired by techniques from coding theory, to construct a robust adaptation framework for unsupervised domain adaptation, by encoding the input target data and generating predictions that are robust against noise and corruption.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Role of Error-Correcting Codes for Robust Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

propositions.controles: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method on several benchmark datasets and compare it against state-of-the-art UDA methods.
propositions.prediction: By leveraging self-supervised representation learning and multi-task learning, we expect that our proposed method can align the feature distributions across domains and achieve state-of-the-art performance on several unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.
propositions.texte: We propose a multi-task learning framework that combines self-supervised representation learning and supervised domain adaptation to align the feature distributions of the source and target domains.
propositions.titre: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Multi-Task Learning with Self-Supervised Representation Alignment

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Conservation Laws into a Neural Graph Solver for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel neural graph solver that embeds conservation laws directly into its architecture, leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to model spatiotemporal dynamics and encoding physical laws as additional nodes in the graph. This approach should significantly reduce the learning space and exploration burden by providing a principled structural foundation for PDE dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and graph-based neural operators on reaction-diffusion dynamics problems.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should exhibit superior performance and data efficiency compared to existing approaches, demonstrating the potential for generalization to unseen source terms. However, challenges may arise when handling complex geometries and boundary conditions, requiring further refinement of the graph architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Graph Architectures to Complex Geometries and Boundary Conditions for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Propose a set of graph architecture modifications, such as multi-resolution graphs, curriculum learning, and adaptive node additions, to better handle complex geometries and boundary conditions in PDE problems. This will enable the neural graph solver to generalize across a broader range of physical systems.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified architectures on a set of validation problems (contaminant transport in channel flow, laser heat treatment) and ablate each modification to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed modifications should significantly improve the solver's ability to handle complex geometries and boundary conditions, leading to improved performance on a variety of PDE problems. However, the additional architectural components may introduce new challenges, such as increased computational overhead and potential overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a Universal Source Term Embedding for Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural source term embedding (NSE) that learns to represent a wide range of source terms in a low-dimensional latent space. The NSE should capture the essential features of source terms, allowing the neural graph solver to generalize to unseen source terms without requiring additional training data.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed NSE with traditional graph-based methods and physics-informed neural networks on a range of PDE problems (light-driven chemical reactions, excitable media) with varying source terms.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The NSE should enable the neural graph solver to generalize to a broader range of source terms, achieving improved performance on a variety of PDE problems. However, challenges may arise when dealing with source terms that possess complex, high-frequency structures, which may not be adequately captured by the NSE.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Learning a Universal Source Term Embedding for Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Refine the Neural Source Term Embedding (NSE) by injecting physical prior knowledge and leverage spectral methods to improve its ability to capture the essential features of source terms. The refined NSE should be more robust and able to generalize to a wider range of PDE problems with varying source terms.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised NSE with the original NSE, as well as with traditional graph-based methods and physics-informed neural networks on a variety of PDE problems.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised NSE should demonstrate improved robustness and ability to generalize to a broader range of PDE problems, but potential challenges may arise when dealing with source terms that exhibit complex, nonlinear behavior or are subject to various scaling factors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISE 2: Adapting Graph Architectures to Complex Geometries and Boundary Conditions for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous proposal by incorporating a novel node pruning strategy during training, to automatically remove nodes that do not contribute significantly to the solution, thus reducing the computational overhead and improving the model's efficiency on complex geometries.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified graph architecture with the original one on a set of validation problems and ablate the node pruning strategy to understand its individual contribution.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed modification should significantly improve the model's efficiency on complex geometries and reduce the computational overhead, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and potential adjustments to the graph architecture.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED 2: Adapting Graph Architectures to Complex Geometries and Boundary Conditions for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal by incorporating a quasi-Monte Carlo (QMCPy) sampling method to efficiently sample the complex geometries and boundary conditions, thus improving the model's ability to generalize to a wider range of PDE problems.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified graph architecture with the original one on a set of validation problems and ablate the QMCPy sampling method to understand its individual contribution.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed modification should significantly improve the model's ability to generalize to complex geometries and boundary conditions, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and potential adjustments to the graph architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness of Neural Graph Solvers to Data Corruption
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of neural graph solvers to data corruption, a common issue in real-world simulations, by introducing random noise or missing data in the training process. This study should help understanding the model's sensitivity to data quality and informing methods to improve its robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare the neural graph solver with traditional PINNs on a range of PDE problems and evaluate their robustness to different levels of data corruption.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The neural graph solver may demonstrate some level of robustness to data corruption, but its overall performance may degrade significantly as the corruption level increases, posing a challenge for its practical deployment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship Between Model Capacity and Generalization in Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Conduct a thorough analysis of the relationship between the model capacity (measured by the number of parameters or the complexity of the architecture) and the generalization performance of neural graph solvers on a wide range of PDE problems. This study should shed light on the importance of model capacity in achieving good generalization.
CONTROLS: Train a set of neural graph solvers with different architectures and capacities on a range of PDE problems and evaluate their generalization performance using metrics such as mean squared error (MSE) and Nash error.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis is likely to reveal a trade-off between model capacity and generalization, where larger models may perform well on the training data but may not generalize well to new data, while smaller models may generalize better but may not perform well on the training data, posing a challenge for designing optimal neural graph solvers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Certified Robustness of Neural Graph Solvers for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of using certified robustness techniques, such as interval arithmetic or abstraction refinement, to provide guarantees on the performance of neural graph solvers on a set of PDE problems, even in the presence of data corruption or model uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Apply certified robustness techniques to a range of neural graph solvers on a set of PDE problems and evaluate their performance using metrics such as certified accuracy and robustness.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The certified robustness techniques may provide a high degree of confidence in the performance of the neural graph solvers, but may also introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Neural Graph Solvers on a Range of PDE Problems
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experimental validation of the proposed neural graph solver on a wide range of PDE problems, including reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport in channel flow, laser heat treatment, and light-driven chemical reactions, using both synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed neural graph solver with traditional PINNs and other state-of-the-art methods on the validation datasets.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The neural graph solver is likely to demonstrate excellent performance on a wide range of PDE problems, with significant improvements over traditional methods, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and potential adjustments to the graph architecture for optimal performance.

CONTROLS: Compare our model with the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) baseline and ablate the impact of individual conservation laws.

Controls: Compare the performance of the hierarchical symmetry encoding with a baseline that uses only low-level or high-level symmetries, evaluate the impact of discounting learned symmetries on adaptation to new PDE systems, and study the effect of fewer distortion on solution crowd mould evolution.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours (modification)
Prediction: Expected to improve the robustness of graph-based PDE solvers to changes in spatial and temporal symmetries, but might become sensitive to noise in the sparse learning procedure and potentially overfit to specific examples of symmetrical PDE systems.

PROPOSAL 4: Multivariate Transfer Learning for Source-Independent Neural PDE Solvers
Develop a multivariate transfer learning framework that learns generalizable source-independent representations across PDE systems and applies the learned representations as a feature extractor to source-dependent PDE solvers, thereby improving transferability and flexibility in source terms.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of transfer learning on source-terms alone and compare with an upper-bound estimate based on worst-case reasoning solvers; investigate the trade-off between generalization and adaptation, and study the deployed quality in multimodal prediction and physical case.
Estimated cost: 220 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to achieve significant improvements in transfer learning and robustness to unseen sources, but might struggle to generalize to complex PDE systems with diverse underlying mechanisms, requiring further work in informal-lower scheme.

PROPOSAL 5: Robust Training and Testing for Neural PDE Solvers via Augmented Physical Noise
Modify the augmented physical noise mechanism in (5) to generate noise that is more geared towards specific sources of uncertainty in the physical system, such as measurement noise, numerical noise, or physics-based errors, and use a novel noise-contrastive learning loss function that incentivizes the neural solver to be robust to these types of noise.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of our modified method on PDE systems where noise has a specific physical origin, compare with our previous method and a baseline method, and investigate the robustness of our method to noise types not seen during training.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours (modification)
Prediction: Expected to demonstrate improved robustness to noise with specific physical origins, but might require additional training time and computational resources to accommodate the modified noise generation and loss function.

PROPOSAL 6: Real-Time Prediction and Dynamics-based Optimization for Neural PDE Solvers
Develop a real-time prediction and optimization framework for neural PDE solvers that leverages the trained solvers to predict system behavior and optimizes control input in real-time, enabling efficient and robust control of complex physical systems.
Controls: Evaluate the performance of the real-time prediction and optimization framework on a range of PDE systems, compare with state-of-the-art control methods, and investigate the computational efficiency of the method.
Estimated cost: 320 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to demonstrate significant improvements in real-time prediction and control performance, but might require additional hardware and software infrastructure to support the real-time optimization and prediction capabilities.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Physics-Informed Neural Network (G-PINN) for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Design a Graph-Physics-Informed Neural Network (G-PINN) that explicitly encodes PDE structural priors, such as graph-based conservation laws, onto graph neural networks (GNNs) and a physics-informed loss function to enforce differential equation residual minimization on irregular spatial domains.
CONTROLS: Compare G-PINN with traditional PINNs and GNNs on synthetic reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and transient heat conduction problems, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and robustness against source term variations.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: G-PINN should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and robustness against source term variations compared to traditional GNNs and PINNs, but it may require additional computational resources due to the complexity of encoding graph-based prior structures into GNNs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Operator-Based Training for Generalization to Unseen Source Terms
PROPOSAL: Introduce an operator-based training framework that explicitly learns mappings between PDE operators and source terms, which enables the solver to generalize to unseen source terms without requiring substantial additional training data.
CONTROLS: Compare the operator-based approach with traditional PINN training on a set of reaction-diffusion problems with varying source terms, evaluating their solution accuracy and generalization capabilities across source terms.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The operator-based approach should demonstrate improved generalization capabilities across source terms, but its solution accuracy may degrade on problems with highly nonlinear or time-varying source terms.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Graph-Physics-Informed Neural Network (G-PINN) for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Enhance the G-PINN architecture by integrating a source-term aware module that conditions the GNN on the given source term, enabling the network to learn problem-specific operator mappings and improving generalization to unseen source terms.
CONTROLS: Compare the enhanced G-PINN with the original G-PINN and the operator-based approach on a set of reaction-diffusion problems with varying source terms, evaluating their solution accuracy and generalization capabilities.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhanced G-PINN should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and generalization capabilities across source terms, but its training complexity may increase due to the additional module, potentially affecting its scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Kartik Graph Neural Network (K-GNN) with Physics-Constrained Structure Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel graph neural network framework, Kartik GNN (K-GNN), that couples physics-constrained structure learning with a graph-partitioning-based approach to model complex spatiotemporal PDE dynamics on irregular domains.
CONTROLS: Compare K-GNN with traditional GNNs, G-PINN, and the operator-based approach on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and laser heat treatment problems, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and robustness against source term variations.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: K-GNN should demonstrate improved solution accuracy, convergence rates, and robustness against source term variations compared to traditional GNNs and other approaches, but its computational complexity may be higher due to the additional structure learning module.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse-Source-Adapted Fourier Neural Operator (SSA-FNO) for Multimodal PDEs
PROPOSAL: Develop a sparse-source-adapted variant of the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) that adaptively selects a reduced set of modes to represent source term variations in multimodal PDEs, mitigating the curse of dimensionality and improving data efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare SSA-FNO with traditional FNO, K-GNN, and other approaches on a set of light-driven chemical reactions and transient heat conduction problems with multiple source term modalities, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and data efficiency.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SSA-FNO should demonstrate improved solution accuracy, convergence rates, and data efficiency on problems with multiple source term modalities, but its mode selection strategy may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Graph-Physics-Informed Neural Network (G-PINN) for PDEs
PROPOSAL: Modify the G-PINN architecture to incorporate a learnable graph partitioning module, enabling the network to adapt the graph structure during training and improving its flexibility in modeling complex PDE dynamics on irregular domains.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised G-PINN with traditional G-PINN, K-GNN, and SSA-FNO on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics and contaminant transport problems with complex geometries, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and robustness against source term variations.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised G-PINN should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and robustness against source term variations on problems with complex geometries, but its training complexity may be higher due to the additional learnable graph partitioning module.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multiresolution Physics-Informed U-Net (MPI-U-Net) for Spatiotemporal PDEs
PROPOSAL: Develop a Multiresolution Physics-Informed U-Net (MPI-U-Net) that leverages a nested architecture and self-attention mechanisms to simultaneously represent high-frequency and low-frequency features in spatiotemporal PDEs, leading to improved solution accuracy and data efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare MPI-U-Net with traditional PINNs, K-GNN, SSA-FNO, and other approaches on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and laser heat treatment problems, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and data efficiency.
COST: 3800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MPI-U-Net should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and data efficiency compared to traditional PINNs and other approaches, but its computational complexity may be higher due to the nested architecture and self-attention mechanisms.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Operator-Based Training for Generalization to Unseen Source Terms
PROPOSAL: Enhance the operator-based training framework by incorporating a uncertainty-aware source-term emulator that estimates the uncertainty of the source term and adapts the operator-based training process to minimize the uncertainty, leading to improved generalization capabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare the enhanced operator-based approach with traditional operator-based training, K-GNN, SSA-FNO, and MPI-U-Net on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics and contaminant transport problems with uncertain source terms, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and robustness against source term variations.
COST: 3200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhanced operator-based approach should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and robustness against source term variations on problems with uncertain source terms, but its training complexity may be higher due to the uncertainty-aware emulator.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Hyperparameter Search for Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Develop a physics-constrained hyperparameter search framework for neural PDE solvers that leverages Bayesian optimization and uncertainty-aware source-term emulators to efficiently search for optimal hyperparameters that balance solution accuracy and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the physics-constrained hyperparameter search framework with traditional random search and grid search on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and laser heat treatment problems, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and computational efficiency.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-constrained hyperparameter search framework should demonstrate improved solution accuracy and computational efficiency compared to traditional hyperparameter search methods, but its computational cost may be higher due to the Bayesian optimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensembled Neural PDE Solver with Uncertainty Quantification
PROPOSAL: Develop an ensembled neural PDE solver that combines the predictions of multiple neural PDE solvers, including the previously proposed models, and provides uncertainty quantification for the solution, enabling robust and reliable predictions even in the presence of uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare the ensembled neural PDE solver with traditional ensembling methods and single neural PDE solvers on a set of reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and laser heat treatment problems, evaluating their solution accuracy, convergence rates, and uncertainty quantification capabilities.
COST: 6000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensembled neural PDE solver should demonstrate improved solution accuracy, convergence rates, and uncertainty quantification capabilities compared to traditional ensembling methods and single neural PDE solvers, but its computational cost may be higher due to the ensemble process.
