actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate the effect of classifier-free guidance on finite-speed Kac flows for conditional image generation, comparing the kinetic energy of the resultant velocity fields to those derived from unconditional sampling, and examining the impact on sample quality and generation speed.
CONTROLS: Baseline - unconditional unconditional Kac flow; Abation - removing guidance completely; Control - compare to a guided conditional diffusion model.
COST: 4320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the guided velocity field to have comparable kinetic energy to unconditional sampling, with a slight degradation in sample quality due to the conditioning process. However, without careful tuning, the guided Kac flow might be unable to achieve the same level of sample quality as the guided diffusion model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One-Step Finite-Speed Generators via Kac Flow Sampling
PROPOSAL: Implement a simple, few-step conditional Kac flow sampler and experimentally compare its sample quality and numerical stability to baseline unconditional and conditional diffusion models, aiming to evaluate whether a one-step finite-speed generator can reach competitive sample quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline - unconditional diffusion; Baseline by construction - unconditional Kac flow; Control - few-step guided diffusion model.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the few-step Kac flow sampler will achieve lower sample quality than baseline models, but the results will show the upper bound of sample quality that can be achieved in a single step with finite-speed flows. Optimizing hyperparameters will be crucial to getting closer to baseline performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 1. Evaluating Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows | 2. Optimal Guidance for Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: 2. Optimal Guidance for Kac Flows: The previous experiment evaluates guidance's impact on kinetic energy, whereas this new experiment designs an optimal guidance scheme tailored to finite-speed flows, ensuring that the guided velocity field remains at low kinetic energy even with conditional sampling. This will involve formulating an optimization problem that controls the gradient of the guidance term to preserve bounded energy.
CONTROLS: Baseline - unconditional Kac flow; Baseline - conventional classifier-free guidance.
COST: 2880 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect optimal guidance to mitigate the kinetic energy blow-up that occurs with conventional guidance, but the optimization process may introduce new challenges or require additional hyperparameter tuning, which could affect the overall sample quality.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows | Optimizing Conditional Kac Flows for One-Step Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop and experimentally evaluate several variants of the one-step Kac flow sampler by optimizing its architecture (e.g., adding layers or improving layer types) or the guidance scheme to improve sample quality and reduce the gap with the baseline few-step diffusion models.
CONTROLS: Baseline - conventional few-step diffusion model; Baseline - few-step unconditional Kac flow; Ablations - examining contributions from separate components of the architecture and guidance.
COST: 4320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating more complex architectures or guidance schemes will lead to improved one-step sample quality, closing some or all of the gap with baseline models. However, there's still a significant possibility that one-step generation will require careful optimization and tailored improvement strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Energy-Based One-Step Kac Flow Sampling
PROPOSAL: Explore whether directly leveraging the finite-speed flow's energy properties can improve one-step sampling, by incorporating energy-based adversarial training or using the kinetic energy of the sampled velocity fields as an additional feedback signal for guiding the sampling process.
CONTROLS: Baseline - conventional one-step Kac flow; Control - few-step diffusion model; Ablations: removing the energy-based feedback signal, replacing it with other methods.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the additional energy-based component to contribute positively to one-step sample quality, possibly closing the gap with a few-step diffusion model, although it may also add complexity and risk instability.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows | Analyzing the Impact of Guidance Optimization on Detailed-Balance Preservation
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the optimal guidance scheme designed for finite-speed flows (from proposal 2) inadvertently breaks the detailed balance condition, which isEssential for preserving the desirable dynamics of the Kac flow, and explore corrective measures to address this issue without sacrificing the guidance's benefits.
CONTROLS: Baseline - unconditional Kac flow; Baseline - conventional classifier-free guidance; Control - few-step diffusion model.
COST: 2880 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that conventional guidance may lead to violations of detailed balance, while the optimal scheme could mitigate these effects, potentially affecting the overall sample quality. Our goal is to determine if additional constraints or modifications can help maintain desirable flow dynamics and try to preserve the benefits of the optimal guidance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Numerical Stability Analysis of Finite-Speed Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: Investigate the numerical stability of finite-speed Kac flows, covering both full-volume noise schedules and few-step samplers with discrete time-steps, by analyzing the smoothness of the velocity field and the flow's contraction coefficient in the Wasserstein distance, as well as characterizing numerically-induced errors.
CONTROLS: Baseline - comparing against unstable unconditional Kac flow; Baseline - comparing against few-step diffusion models.
COST: 4320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the finite-speed Kac flow to exhibit improved numerical stability compared to diffusion due to its bounded-energy structure and causal propagation speed. However, specific formulations of one-step sampling could exacerbate these effects, requiring further analysis and improvements for optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows | Quantifying the Trade-Off between Modified Guidance and Degraded Kac Flow Stability
PROPOSAL: Re-evaluate the optimal guidance scheme designed for finite-speed flows, now taking into account the insights gained from numerical stability analysis, to quantify any potential trade-offs between guidance improvement and the flow's stability, and explore refinements to maintain desirable flow properties.
CONTROLS: Baseline - conventional unconditional Kac flow; Baseline - conventional few-step diffusion model with classifier-free guidance; Ablations: removing the initial guidance optimization; sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters related to guiding schemes.
COST: 4032 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating numerical stability considerations into the guidance optimization will modify the obtained guidance, affecting both sample quality and the bounded-energy property, and conclude whether improved stability can be achieved, and what the limits of this trade-off may be.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Probabilistic Guarantees for Finite-Speed Kac Flow Samplers
PROPOSAL: Derive probabilistic bounds on the performance of the finite-speed Kac flow sampler under realistic assumptions, such as noisy or incomplete data, and relatively small sampler memory, and leveraging the ODEs' structure, to provide theoretical guarantees for its performance and suggest conditions for reliable operation.
CONTROLS: Baseline - deriving bounds for current Kac flow sampler; Control - existing results for diffusion-based models; Ablations: relaxing conditions for sampler performance.
COST: 5184 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the improved probabilistic guarantees to be aligned with observed behaviors in the previous experiments and provide a more solid theoretical foundation for practical usage of finite-speed flow samplers, highlighting key requirements and design considerations. However, enforcing these conditions might introduce additional overhead and limit flexibility in sampler operation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fast Low-Latency Sampling for Conditional Finite-Speed Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: Develop a high-performance implementation of the one-step finite-speed Kac flow sampler with efficient numerical integration, reduced memory footprint, and optimized API for easy integration with existing frameworks, and demonstrate improved performance on real-world image generation tasks compared to current state-of-the-art diffusion-based generators.
CONTROLS: Baseline - conventional few-step diffusion models; Control - evaluating performance under various hardware configurations.
COST: 8640 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our optimized Kac flow sampler will obtain competitive performance in terms of sample quality and generation speed, offering a new direction for image generation that balances efficiency, numerical stability, and optimization requirements. However, achieving reliable, twofold speedup will challenge solver strategies and coupling engine implementation.

TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of LLM-based Time Series Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: Train a range of pre-trained LLMs (e.g., T5, BART, and related transformer models) on a diverse set of text-to-text and time series-to-text tasks, exploring their ability to capture relevant time series features and quality characteristics. Perform ablative analyses of the influence of prompt design and the choice of pre-trained LLM.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include a range of existing domain-specific quality estimation methods, such as RNN-based time series models, and simple domain-agnostic methods such as the proportion of missing values in the time series.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see some degree of performance across different LLMs, with better results for more diverse pre-training datasets, and large datasets of diverse text series examples. Where it could fail: emerging inconsistencies across LLMs render the performance unreliable.

TITLE: Time Series Quality Estimation with LLM-based Prompt Engineering

"Exploring LLM-Prompted Time Series Quality Estimation via Controlled Semantics Search"
PROPOSAL: Design a controlled semantics search framework that leverages off-the-shelf LLMs (e.g., T5, code T5) to identify the most informative subset of text prompts that can effectively capture key features of high-quality time series data. We will train LLM-based quality estimators on synthetic and real-world time series data, focusing on diverse domains such as electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, and traffic forecasting. The proposed framework will use a search algorithm (e.g., Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning) to find the optimal combinations of prompts and supervise the quality estimator with a proxy objective function that balances accuracy and efficiency.

TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Pre-Trained LLMs in Time Series Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: Design a large-scale comparison study to evaluate the effectiveness of pre-trained LLMs (e.g., T5, switching variants) in time series quality estimation tasks. We will train and evaluate multiple LLM-based quality estimators on synthetic and real-world time series datasets from diverse domains (e.g., electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting). The study will investigate the impact of pre-training objectives, model sizes, and prompt engineering on the quality estimation accuracy across different domains. We will also assess the transferability of pre-trained LLMs across various time series settings, to identify the most effective architectures for general-purpose quality estimation.

COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours for multi-endpoint pretraining and evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Pretrained LLMs for Time Series Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the quality assessment capabilities of a selection of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) - including T5 and BART - on a diverse set of time series datasets across various domains (electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting, weather forecasting, handwriting recognition, spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection) and estimate the limitations of their judgments.
CONTROLS: Compare against human judgments (via crowdsourcing or precedent expert evaluations), ablating and varying the input format (time series converted to text, specific quality criteria embedded in prompts), assessing sensitivity to training data size and available information about the time series.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the trained LLMs to perform reasonably well on directly relevant quality assessment tasks, but struggle on non-obvious and abstract dimensions of quality, such as highlighting continuity and temporal dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Domain-Agnostic Prompts for Time Series Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of domain-agnostic, time series quality evaluation prompts based on a detailed analysis of quality characteristics across diverse domains, such as continuity, completeness, stationarity, and temporal dependencies, and evaluate the efficacy of these prompts on various pretrained LLMs using the same datasets as in (1), as well as additional real-world datasets to validate their generalizability. Identifying essential quality characteristics common across domains can provide the foundation for time series quality evaluation at scale.
CONTROLS: Establish the quality criteria used in evaluation prompts, select and provide domain-specific exemplary datasets for validation, contrast with results from (1) to determine performance augmentation due to the improved prompts. Evaluate human judgments using pairs of written explanations for the prompts to verify how good an LLM or human assessment  correctly supports the given random selection of criteria, especially at being predominant or not  when those criteria are suitable for markup.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved LLM performance on quality assessment tasks; scalable and interpretable.

This approach can exploit the fact that some quality characteristics (e.g. continuity, stationarity) are shared across domains.

TITLE: Human-in-the-Loop Quality Evaluation andVerification
PROPOSAL: To improve the accuracy and robustness of time series quality evaluation, design a human-in-the-loop (HITL) approach where human evaluators assess and annotate time series data, and LLMs learn from these annotations. This feedback loop will enable the LLMs to adapt and improve over time, as they learn to distinguish between high-quality and low-quality time series data.
CONTROLS: Compare HITL performance with solely LLM-based evaluation, evaluate the effectiveness of different human-LLM interaction modalities (e.g., active learning, cost-sensitive sampling), examine the impact of HITL on LLM model interpretability and explainability.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Digraph Generators with a Customized Directed Graph Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Develop a new benchmark suite (DirGen-Benchmark) specifically for evaluating the quality of directed graph generators, consisting of a diverse set of synthetic digraphs across various topological structures and densities, with accompanying GT (ground truth) labels and evaluation metrics. The benchmark will feature two types of graphs: (a) regular graphs with controlled topological features (e.g., symmetry, trees, cycles), and (b) sparse, noisy graphs representative of real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Use undirected graph benchmarks like MolGAN (generative model for molecular graphs) as weak baseline, and ensure the proposed benchmark's performance does not regress significantly when compared to strong baseline methods (e.g., recent directed graph generative models)
COST: 10 GPU-hours (only synthetic data, no computationally expensive generation methods required)
PREDICTION: DirGen-Benchmark will serve as a reliable, open-source benchmark for evaluating directed graph generators, highlighting differences in performance across various topological structures and allowing for fair comparisons among methods. However, we might encounter issues when generalizing to real-world datasets with distinctive structural properties not present in the benchmark.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Directed Graph Variant Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of two different autoencoder architectures, applying them to our proposed DirGen-Benchmark and assessing their ability to preserve structural properties and directional dependencies in generated digraphs: (1) a plain Graph Autoencoder (GAE) for directed graphs and (2) a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) variant that is aware of the graph's directionality. The goal is to see if the latter enables better performance on tasks like digraph classification, clustering, and generation of realistic digraphs.
CONTROLS: Experiment with both plain GAE and GCN-based variants, using DirGen-Benchmark for rigorous comparison and testing the performance of each on a range of tasks; include a baseline comparing the approach to random or straightforward models.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training and testing of each model on the synthetic benchmark)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements from using a GCN-based variant over a standard GAE, particularly in maintaining directed relationships. However, we might experience performance degradation if the weight or configuration are mishandled for the GCN case.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Improving Digraph Generation with Multi-Stage Evolutionary Search
PROPOSAL: Develop and apply a multi-stage evolutionary algorithm (EA) approach to search for architectures of directed graph generators, using the DirGen-Benchmark to evaluate candidate models. The approach will involve a combination of pre-evaluation and fine-tuning: (1) an initial population of candidate architectures is generated randomly; (2) these candidates are evaluated using predefined metrics (e.g., edge accuracy, node-degree complexity); and (3) the fittest candidates are re-seed and replaced by generating new candidates using advanced crossover, mutation, and recombination operators, aiming to converge to optimal architectures for digraph generation. 
CONTROLS: Compare EA results with gradient-based optimization methods (e.g., ADADELTA) and assess performance on synthetic digraphs for the final candidate model as well as comparison to the results using variant autoencoders (experiment 2).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (training, testing, and EA on the synthetic benchmark)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the EA approach will lead to improved digraph generation results, mainly due to a more deliberate search strategy for discovering model architectures. If the crossover and mutation steps are not carefully designed, we may end up with ineffective search operators, such as local optima.

TITLE: Applying Neural Architecture Search (NAS) for Optimizing Directed Graph Generators
PROPOSAL: Utilize Neural Architecture Search (NAS) techniques to optimize the architectures of directed graph generators, aiming to find the optimal model configuration for the DirGen-Benchmark: (1) use a reinforcement learning-based NAS (RL-NAS) method to search for the best architecture; (2) incorporate the DirGen-Benchmark into the NAS framework to evaluate the performance of candidate architectures; (3) compare the performance of the NAS-optimized models to the state-of-the-art directed graph generators.

CONTROLS: Use the results from Experiment 6 to guide the NAS search process, and explore the impact of different regularization techniques on the performance of the NAS-optimized DGVAE variants.

However, the search process may be computationally expensive, and the resulting models may not generalize well to real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Generated Digraphs in Scene Graph Generation Tasks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the generated digraphs using a directed graph generator (DGG) trained on the DirGen-Benchmark, in the context of scene graph generation tasks, specifically on the Visual Genome dataset: (1) generate digraphs using the DGG; (2) convert the digraphs to scene graphs; (3) compare the performance of the generated scene graphs with existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of object detection, relationship classification, and scene understanding metrics.
CONTROLS: Use the results from the previous experiments as the input to this experiment, and compare the performance of the directed graph generator with other strong baseline methods.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (generating and evaluating digraphs and scene graphs)
PREDICTION: We expect that the generated scene graphs will show improved performance on object detection, relationship classification, and scene understanding tasks, and provide insights into the effectiveness of using directed graph generators for scene understanding tasks. However, the performance may be affected by the quality of the generated digraphs and the ability of the scene graph generation task to utilize the directed relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Recurrent Models for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of baseline experiments to evaluate the performance of recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures (LSTM, GRU) in generating directed graphs, including both acyclic and cyclic graphs, with and without structural constraints. We will use a combination of established metrics to evaluate the generated graphs, including adjacency matrix similarity, structural embedder (SD) loss, and graph centrality metrics (e.g., degree, betweenness, closeness centrality). We will also compare the performance of different RNN architectures and recurrent flavors (e.g., 1D, 2D, temporal convolutional) to assess the impact of modeling choices on generative quality.
CONTROLS: Existing autoencoder-based approaches for directed graph generation, specifically GARCH and DGAE, with two ablation studies: (1) varying the number of time steps in the RNN model, and (2) using different embedding schemes to capture node relationships.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will challenge the state of the art in directed graph generation, specifically in the evaluation of RNN models and their recurrent flavors, and will provide insights into the role of structural constraints in graph generation. We anticipate a moderate performance gap between state-of-the-art DGAE and our proposed RNN models, with LSTM performing better than GRU.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in capturing cycled graphs due to limitations in current recursive models (by comparison with srGNN, an edge-RNN reportedly showed effective generation capabilities in this area)
(b) modeling node and graph meta-properties with sufficient autonomy;

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Transformers for Directed Graph Generation
PROPOSAL: Given the success of Transformers in various sequence and graph-based tasks, we propose to investigate their applicability to directed graph generation, specifically when using self-attention mechanisms to model node and edge relationships. We will employ the Transformer-XL architecture, which is designed for long-range dependencies, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art RNN models, including those proposed in experiment 1. We will also modify the Transformer-XL architecture to incorporate edge features and directionality explicitly, and evaluate its impact on generative quality.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's baseline RNN models, DGAE, and two additional ablation studies: (1) using a standard Transformer model instead of the more advanced Transformer-XL, and (2) comparing the performance of self-supervised and supervised learning strategies for Transformer-XL.
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the Transformer-XL will outperform some RNN models, especially for larger graphs, due to its ability to model long-range dependencies and parallelize computations. However, our modified Transformer-XL may not achieve the state of the art in generative quality, and we may see limitations in its ability to capture cyclical graph structures.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in adapting self-attention mechanisms to directed graph generation, potentially leading to overcounting or overemphasizing edge directions; 
(b) relying solely on self-supervised or supervised learning may not allow the model to effectively capture the directional structure of graphs.

PROPOSAL 1: Evaluating Recurrent Models for Directed Graph Generation
We propose a set of baseline experiments to evaluate the performance of recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures (LSTM, GRU) in generating directed graphs, including both acyclic and cyclic graphs, with and without structural constraints. We will use a combination of established metrics to evaluate the generated graphs, including adjacency matrix similarity, structural embedder (SD) loss, and graph centrality metrics (e.g., degree, betweenness, closeness centrality). We will also compare the performance of different RNN architectures and recurrent flavors (e.g., 1D, 2D, temporal convolutional) to assess the impact of modeling choices on generative quality.
Controls: Existing autoencoder-based approaches for directed graph generation, specifically GARCH and DGAE, with two ablation studies: (1) varying the number of time steps in the RNN model, and (2) using different embedding schemes to capture node relationships.
Estimated cost: 10,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our results will challenge the state of the art in directed graph generation, specifically in the evaluation of RNN models and their recurrent flavors, and will provide insights into the role of structural constraints in graph generation. We anticipate a moderate performance gap between state-of-the-art DGAE and our proposed RNN models, with LSTM performing better than GRU.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in capturing cycled graphs due to limitations in current recursive models (by comparison with srGNN, an edge-RNN reportedly showed effective generation capabilities in this area)
(b) modeling node and graph meta-properties with sufficient autonomy;

PROPOSAL 2: Investigating the Feasibility of Transformers for Directed Graph Generation
Given the success of Transformers in various sequence and graph-based tasks, we propose to investigate their applicability to directed graph generation, specifically when using self-attention mechanisms to model node and edge relationships. We will employ the Transformer-XL architecture, which is designed for long-range dependencies, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art RNN models, including those proposed in experiment 1. We will also modify the Transformer-XL architecture to incorporate edge features and directionality explicitly, and evaluate its impact on generative quality.
Controls: Experiment 1's baseline RNN models, DGAE, and two additional ablation studies: (1) using a standard Transformer model instead of the more advanced Transformer-XL, and (2) comparing the performance of self-supervised and supervised learning strategies for Transformer-XL.
Estimated cost: 15,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We anticipate that the Transformer-XL will outperform some RNN models, especially for larger graphs, due to its ability to model long-range dependencies and parallelize computations. However, our modified Transformer-XL may not achieve the state of the art in generative quality, and we may see limitations in its ability to capture cyclical graph structures.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in adapting self-attention mechanisms to directed graph generation, potentially leading to overcounting or overemphasizing edge directions; 
(b) relying solely on self-supervised or supervised learning may not allow the model to effectively capture the directional structure of graphs.

PROPOSAL 3: Incorporating Domain Knowledge for Directed Graph Generation
We refine our proposal by focusing on scene graph generation as the primary target application, and integrate the structural embedding module with a node filtering process to preserve acyclicity. We will extend our evaluation to include more real-world scene graph datasets, such as Visual Genome and Google Open Images Extended, and compare our results with state-of-the-art models for scene graph generation. We will also investigate the impact of different node filtering techniques, such as LIFO and Priority Queues, on generative quality.
Controls: Experiment 1's baseline RNN models, experiment 2's Transformer models, and three additional ablation studies: (1) comparing our node filtering approach with popular state-of-the-art graph generation models, (2) evaluating the impact of different node filtering techniques on performance, and (3) assessing the effect of varying the strength of the node filtering process on generated graph quality.
Estimated cost: 20,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We anticipate that incorporating domain knowledge will significantly improve generative quality on real-world scene graph generation tasks, compared to state-of-the-art models. Our results will also highlight the crucial role of node filtering in preserving structural constraints in generated graphs.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in effectively capturing nuanced structural properties of real-world scene graphs; 
(b) increased parameter and computational complexity of the node filtering process.

To improve the robustness and quality of directed graph generators, we propose to incorporate adversarial training into our pipeline. We will use a GAN-based approach to encourage the generator to produce graphs that are indistinguishable from real graphs in terms of structural and semantic properties. We will evaluate the impact of adversarial training on the generator's performance on downstream tasks and compare it with traditional training approaches.

(b) potential overfitting to specific graph characteristics or adversarial attacks.

We refine our proposal by incorporating the insights gained from our previous experiments and incorporating multi-task learning into our framework in a more integrated way. We will assume that multiple tasks share a common representation space and adapt our gradients of a multi-headed (multitasking) generator for optimization of the structure prediction path.

Expected failure points: 
(a) difficulty in designing effective task combinations for multi-task learning, potentially leading to degradation in task performance; 
(b) potential overfitting to specific tasks or task combinations, leading to decreased robustness.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Flow-Based Solver for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: Design a neural network architecture based on the IMF scheme to solve the tree-structured SB problem for star-shaped trees with fixed marginals on the leaves and an unknown centre. The architecture will consist of a series of neural ODEs/SDEs, each corresponding to a node in the tree, with message passing between nodes to preserve the marginals at each iteration. We will use the Brownian motion as the reference process and train the architecture using the entropy-regularised loss.
CONTROLS: We will compare our solver with the IPF-based diffusion SB approach and a naively designed neural baseline, both of which will be implemented using a similar neural ODE/SDE architecture but without the message passing mechanism.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our solver to converge to the tree-structured SB solution in fewer iterations than the IPF-based approach and demonstrate reduced training instability at low entropic regularisation, while producing a comparable or better Wasserstein-2 barycentre estimate to the fixed-point method for the barycentre problem. This may fail if the IMF scheme implementation is not correctly integrated with the neural ODE/SDE architecture, leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Fixed-Point and Flow-Based Methods for Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: Empirically compare the convergence of the existing fixed-point method and the flow-based solver proposed in proposal 1 for computing tree-structured SB solutions and Wasserstein-2 barycentres. We will track the maximum mean squared difference between the estimated barycentre and the true barycentre, obtained using the exact Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation for a simple star-shaped tree with fixed marginals on the leaves.
CONTROLS: We will also compare the fixed-point and flow-based methods with respect to computational time and memory usage, as well as provide a sanity check by comparing the results with ground-truth barycentre obtained using a simple it=0 starting guess without entropic regularization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: We expect the flow-based solver to converge to the tree-structured SB solution with fewer iterations than the fixed-point method, but with increased computational time due to the complexity of the IMF scheme. However, this may fail if the chosen neural ODE/SDE architecture and training objectives are not optimal for this problem, leading to slower convergence than the fixed-point method.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Developing a Flow-Based Solver for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: On top of the architecture described in proposal 1, we will explore different types of message passing between nodes to further improve the performance of the flow-based solver. Specifically, we will investigate:
- Local message passing, where messages are passed between directly connected nodes in the tree.
- Multiscale message passing, where messages are passed between nodes at different scales in the tree, and
- Hierarchical message passing, where messages are passed between nodes in a hierarchical structure within each tree.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of these different message passing variants with the original architecture and discuss the trade-offs between computational cost and accuracy.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical and multiscale message passing variants to improve the performance of the flow-based solver by providing a more efficient way to preserve the marginals at each node, especially as the tree becomes deeper or more complex. However, this may fail if the more complex message passing schemes are computationally expensive or difficult to implement.

PROPOSAL: On top of the architecture described in proposal 1, we will explore different types of message passing between nodes to further improve the performance of the flow-based solver. Specifically, we will investigate:
- Local message passing, where messages are passed between directly connected nodes in the tree.
- Multiscale message passing, where messages are passed between nodes at different scales in the tree, and
- Hierarchical message passing, where messages are passed between nodes in a hierarchical structure within each tree.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of these different message passing variants with the original architecture and discuss the trade-offs between computational cost and accuracy.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical and multiscale message passing variants to improve the performance of the flow-based solver by providing a more efficient way to preserve the marginals at each node, especially as the tree becomes deeper or more complex. However, this may fail if the more complex message passing schemes are computationally expensive or difficult to implement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Studying the Impact of Tree Structure on Flow-Based SB Computation
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the structure of the tree affects the performance of the flow-based solver for tree-structured SB problems. We will consider various tree structures, such as star-shaped trees, binary trees, and trees with a varying number of nodes and connections. For each tree structure, we will compare the convergence rate, accuracy, and computational cost of the flow-based solver with different message passing schemes.
CONTROLS: We will use synthetic data generated using a range of tree structures with prescribed marginals at the leaves and compare the results with the exact Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation for a simple star-shaped tree.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the performance of the flow-based solver to be influenced by the tree structure, with star-shaped trees and tree structures with fewer connections being computationally more efficient than more complex structures. However, this may fail if the chosen message passing scheme does not effectively adapt to the tree structure, leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Hierarchical Processing of Flow-Based Tree-Structured SB
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical processing framework to facilitate the scalability of the flow-based solver for tree-structured SB problems. This framework will utilize a divide-and-conquer approach, dividing the problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved independently, and subsequently combining the results to obtain the overall solution. We will apply this framework to trees with a large number of nodes and complex structures and study its effects on convergence rate, accuracy, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare the hierarchical processing framework with a naive approach that visits the nodes in the tree sequentially and discuss the trade-offs between scalability and accuracy.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical processing framework to significantly improve the scalability of the flow-based solver, enabling it to handle large tree structures with a large number of nodes. However, this may fail if the divide-and-conquer approach leads to increased communication overhead between sub-problems or a loss of accuracy in the joint solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Wasserstein Barycentre Computation for Hierarchical Data Structures
PROPOSAL: Adapt the flow-based solver for tree-structured SB problems to compute Wasserstein barycentres of hierarchical data structures, such as dendrograms and hierarchical clusters. We will design a method to recursively compute the barycentre at each level of the hierarchy, using the flow-based solver to compute the local barycentre at each node. We will use the Manhattan and Euclidean tree structures as benchmarks to validate the proposed method.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed flow-based approach with traditional barycentre computation methods, such as iterative fixed-point methods and hierarchical clustering, and discuss the trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, and interpretability.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed flow-based approach to provide a more efficient and accurate method for computing Wasserstein barycentres of hierarchical data structures, especially for large and complex hierarchies. However, this may fail if the recursive computation of the local barycentre leads to numerical instability or a loss of accuracy in the overall barycentre estimate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Wasserstein Barycentre Computation for Bike-Rental Count Regression
PROPOSAL: Apply the flow-based solver to compute the Wasserstein barycentre of a set of bike-rental count distributions, each corresponding to a different time of day in the city. We will use a star-shaped tree structure to model the hierarchical relationships between the time-of-day distributions and compute the barycentre at the root node. We will evaluate the performance of the flow-based approach using regression metrics, such as mean absolute error and mean squared error, and compare it with traditional regression methods.
CONTROLS: We will use the Paris bike-rental dataset and compare the performance of the flow-based approach with supervised regression and clustering methods, including hierarchical clustering and K-medians.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the flow-based barycentre computation to improve the accuracy of the bike-rental count regression model compared to traditional regression methods, particularly for large and complex datasets. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge for Wasserstein Barycentres
PROPOSAL: Implement a flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger bridge (TSB-SB) solver using the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, extending the recent success of IMF-based flow solvers to the tree-structured SB problem. This will involve coupling a neural network with a tree-structured Markov process, which will learn to transform the input distribution through the edge dynamics and vertex marginals of the star-shaped tree.
CONTROLS: The baseline will be the existing IPF-based neural ODE/SDE barycentre solver in the multi-marginal TSB setting, and to understand the impact of IMF on convergence, ablate the IMF scheme and compare to a vanilla IMF-based flow solver.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the IMF-based TSB-SB solver to converge stably and efficiently to the tree-structured SB solution, achieving superior marginal fidelity and faster training times compared to the IPF-based solver. Satisfaction of the assumptions of the theoretical guarantees is expected, but empirical results may deviate in practice due to approximation errors in the neural network.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Flow-based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge for Wasserstein Barycentres (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify Proposal 1 to include a conditional normalising flow component, allowing the IMF-based TSB-SB solver to efficiently model complex transitions between the vertex marginals by transforming samples from a conditionally normalised distribution.
CONTROLS: The ablations will include a vanilla IMF-based flow solver without the conditional normalising flow, and an experiment with the existing IPF-based solver using conditional normalising flows to improve marginal fidelity.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (additional 100 GPU-hours for the new ablation and additional complexity of the CNAF)
PREDICTION: By incorporating conditional normalising flows into the IMF-based TSB-SB solver, we expect to significantly improve marginal fidelity without sacrificing stability and convergence speed, achieving state-of-the-art results for the Wasserstein barycentre problem. However, the additional complexity of the CNAF might lead to increased training times, and extrapolating to practical applications may be challenging without further validation.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Flow-based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge for Wasserstein Barycentres (Revised)
PROPOSAL: In addition to the conditional normalising flow component, incorporate an iterative fixed-point method to the IMF-based TSB-SB solver to leverage the strength of fixed-point schemes and the scalability of flow-based methods. This will involve repeatingly updating a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps, while training the flow to improve the inter-mediate distributions at every iteration.
CONTROLS: The baseline will be the existing IPF-based neural ODE/SDE barycentre solver in the multi-marginal TSB setting, and to understand the impact of the iterative fixed-point method on convergence, ablate both the IMF scheme and the iterative fixed-point method.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining the strengths of flow-based methods and fixed-point schemes, we expect to achieve fast and stable convergence to the tree-structured SB solution, while maintaining or even improving marginal fidelity compared to the IPF-based solver. However, evaluating convergence and proposed solution stability may require additional care due to the multi-stage nature of the solver.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Empirical Analysis of the Flow-based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: Perform an in-depth empirical analysis of the revised flow-based tree-structured Schrödinger bridge (TSB-SB) solver by evaluating its scalability, convergence properties, and computational efficiency on synthetic and synthetic datasets of gradually increasing complexity and dimensionality. This will involve carefully benchmarking the solver on a variety of experimental settings and dataset sizes, comparing against state-of-the-art methods for Wasserstein barycentres, and studying its performance as a function of key hyperparameters and solver configurations.
CONTROLS: The experiments will be controlled against a set of baseline methods, including the existing IPF-based neural ODE/SDE barycentre solver, the vanilla IMF-based flow solver, and a recent multi-level method for Wasserstein barycentres.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis is expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver in real-world settings and under various experimental conditions. However, conducting this analysis is computationally expensive, and edges of the solver's performance may be explored in the near future only in part or under approximation, potentially ignoring outliers or edge cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-based Barycentre Computation for High-dimensional Data
PROPOSAL: Develop a flow-based method for computing the Wasserstein barycentre of two high-dimensional probability distributions, leveraged by the capabilities of the proposed revised flow-based TSB-SB solver. This will involve evolving a sequence of intermediate distributions, parameterized by the flow, to compute the Wasserstein barycentre. We aim to demonstrate its ability to handle high-dimensional data, such as real-world image or audio datasets.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be the existing multi-level method for Wasserstein barycentres, comparing the performance of the flow-based method to this established approach in both speed and quality of results.

TITLE: Improved Variational Formulation and Regularization for Wasserstein Barycentres
PROPOSAL: Develop a new variational formulation for the Wasserstein barycentre problem, using the concepts of optimal transport and Schrödinger bridges. This formulation will incorporate regularization terms to improve the stability and convergence of barycentre estimation. A corresponding neural network architecture will be designed to approximate the solution of the variational problem, leveraging the strengths of neural networks in handling high-dimensional distributions.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be the existing iterative fixed-point method for Wasserstein barycentres, comparing the performance of the new variational formulation to this established approach in terms of convergence speed, marginal fidelity, and computational efficiency.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours

However, the design of the neural network architecture and the adaptation of the regularization terms to the specific problem may pose computational challenges and require tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Subset Posterior Aggregation via Wasserstein Barycentres
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of Wasserstein barycentres for Bayesian subset posterior aggregation in the context of Bayesian inference for bike-rental count regression. This will involve computing the Wasserstein barycentre of posterior distributions obtained from sub-sampled data, using the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver. The resulting barycentre will serve as a representative posterior distribution for the full dataset, enabling accurate predictive inference on unobserved instances.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be a recent method for Bayesian subset posterior aggregation, comparing the performance of the Wasserstein barycentre approach to this established method in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the strengths of Wasserstein barycentres for posterior aggregation, we expect to obtain accurate and representative posterior distributions on the bike-rental count regression task, despite sub-sampling the data. However, optimizing the computation of the barycentre for this specific task might introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Barycentre Robustness and Stability with Adversarial Transport
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness and stability of the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver and the corresponding Wasserstein barycentres by introducing adversarial transport, where small perturbations in the marginals or the reference distribution lead to significant changes in the barycentre. This will involve developing an adversarial training approach to quantify the sensitivity of the solver to such perturbations and to analyze its convergence properties in the presence of noise.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be the existing IPF-based neural ODE/SDE barycentre solver, comparing the robustness and stability of the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver to this more established method.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing the robustness and stability of the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver with adversarial transport, we expect to provide a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential vulnerabilities of the method, as well as a more comprehensive evaluation of its performance in the presence of noise. However, designing an effective adversarial training approach may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-level Optimization for Scalable and Accurate Wasserstein Barycentre Computation
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-level optimization approach to efficiently compute Wasserstein barycentres on large-scale datasets by iteratively refining the solution at multiple scales. This will involve adapting the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver to a multi-level framework, where the solver is applied to progressively refined versions of the data, with the goal of improving both the accuracy and computational efficiency of the barycentre computation.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be a recent multi-level method for Wasserstein barycentres, comparing the performance of the multi-level optimization approach to this established method in terms of both speed and accuracy.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating multi-level optimization into the revised flow-based TSB-SB solver, we expect to significantly improve the scalability and accuracy of Wasserstein barycentre computation, enabling more efficient and representative inference on large-scale datasets. However, designing the multi-level framework may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and potentially introducing additional computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Wasserstein Barycentres and Optimal Transport on Bayesian Models
PROPOSAL: Unify the various components and techniques developed throughout the paper into a comprehensive framework for computing Wasserstein barycentres and optimal transport on Bayesian models, leveraging the strengths of flow-based methods, multi-level optimization, and adversarial transport. This framework will provide a flexible and scalable approach to Bayesian inference, enabling robust and accurate estimation of posterior distributions for complex models and large-scale datasets.
CONTROLS: The control baseline will be a range of existing methods for Bayesian inference and optimal transport, comparing the performance of the unified framework to these established approaches in terms of speed, accuracy, and scalability.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By consolidating the advances made in this paper into a unified framework, we expect to provide a powerful and flexible tool for Bayesian inference, enabling researchers and practitioners to tackle challenging problems in a wide range of domains. However, thoroughly testing and validating the framework may require significant computational resources and expertise.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Flow-Based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge Solver with Guaranteed Convergence
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel flow-based solver for the tree-structured Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem, leveraging the advantages of Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme. Our approach, dubbed "Flow-IMF," incorporates an auxiliaryODE-based strategy to ensure convergence to the SB solution for any tree-structured cost, including star-shaped trees with unknown centre. Numerical stability and efficiency are achieved through adaptive step-size control and caching.
CONTROLS: We compare Flow-IMF against a baseline of the IPF-based diffusion SB solver, with ablations testing the efficacy of the auxiliary ODE strategy and step-size control. For a fair comparison, we limit the baseline solver's entropic regularisation to a range that eliminates the reported instability, to verify whether the challenges prevailing in the original report are inherent.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Flow-IMF is expected to yield clean and stable convergence to the SB solution across diverse star-shaped tree structures, producing Wasserstein-2 barycentres that match the prescribed marginals precisely. However, we anticipate difficulties in reproducing the baseline's dramatic instability if entropic regularisation is low, although our predictions will ensure the accuracy of our auxiliary ODE addition.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Efficient Fast Convergence for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: To investigate whether the fast convergence observed in fixed-point schemes can be harnessed with our flow-based solver, we explore the adaptation of Flow-IMF to incorporate a convergence-preserving fixed-point iteration with overlapping sweeps, analogous to the iterative fixed-point method used for Wasserstein-2 barycentres. This extension, dubbed "Flow-IMF*," maintains the advantages of Flow-IMF while retaining fast convergence.
CONTROLS: We baseline Flow-IMF* against Flow-IMF and the original IPF-based SB solver, exploring the impact of the number of iterations and overlapping sweeps on convergence speed and accuracy. For an in-depth analysis, we also include an ablation that eliminates any prior stabilisation of the original solver, providing a direct comparison of performance in the absence of auxiliary ODE guidance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to retain fast convergence of the fixed-point scheme while comparing favourably to the baseline solver on speed and iteration count. Its performance is expected to be more impacted by low entropic regularisation, although step-size control should help counteract potential instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Wasserstein-2 Barycentre Computation via Neural ODE Backpropagation
PROPOSAL: To bridge the gap between the fixed-point iterative method and the flow-based Schrödinger bridge solver, we derive a novel neural ODE-based approach to computing Wasserstein-2 barycentres for tree-structured marginals. Our method leverages the stability and scalability benefits of Flow-IMF* to compute the required OT maps, which are then combined through weighted averages to estimate the barycentre.
CONTROLS: We investigate this approach in comparison to fixed-point iterative methods (including the previous baseline), the Flow-IMF* solver, and the state-of-the-art neural parameterisation methods for barycentre computation, which require multi-level or adversarial optimisation. For a consolidated test of barycentre quality, we use real-world Bayesian posterior aggregation tasks involving bike-rental count regression.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to overcome the scalability challenges faced by existing neural parameterisation methods, providing efficient and accurate estimates of Wasserstein-2 barycentres with real-world applications. However, we anticipate that lower entropic regularisation could compromise the stability of the neural ODE solver, necessitating further investigation.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Efficient Fast Convergence for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge
PROPOSAL: To refine our previous extension incorporating a convergence-preserving fixed-point iteration with overlapping sweeps, dubbed "Flow-IMF*," we now include an estimated Schrödinger bridge loss as an additional stabilising term in the solver's objective function. This novel Adaptation of Flow-IMF*, dubbed "Flow-IMF**," exploits the benefits of both fixed-point and probabilistic modelling schemes, merging the convergence properties of the former and the stability benefits of the latter.
CONTROLS: We maintain the comparison with Flow-IMF, the IPF-based SB solver, and investigate the added value of this adaptation by evaluating its impact on computational time, convergence speed, and accuracy of the resulting Wasserstein-2 barycentres. The entropic regularisation bracket is adjusted to surpass that initially reported to cause difficulties, ensuring a comprehensive validation of the Flow-IMF** adaptation.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Flow-IMF** is expected to overcome the performance limitations faced by the original adaptation, showcasing consistent and fast convergence with real-world applications of Wasserstein-2 barycentres. Special emphasis is placed on performance in scenarios with low entropic regularisation, with Flow-IMF** demonstrating greater resilience.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Flow-Based Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge Solver with Guaranteed Convergence
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous work, we introduce a hybrid framework for Flow-IMF that combines the advantages of explicit Schrödinger bridge learning with implicit numerical integration. This enhancement, dubbed "Hybrid Flow-IMF," exploits the parameterisations offered by the neural ODEs recently explored in Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation to improve the prior stabilisation of Flow-IMF.
CONTROLS: We compare Hybrid Flow-IMF against the original Flow-IMF and the improved IPF-based SB solver to evaluate the viability of explicit-implicit strategies in tree-structured problems. We also explore ablations to assess the influence of indirect stabilisation on solver stability and convergence properties.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved robustness and faster convergence compared to the baseline Flow-IMF, especially in star-shaped tree configurations where stabilising factor becomes a challenging bottleneck to cross.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Hierarchical MOT: A Multi-Level Flow-Based OT Solver for Scalable Barycentre Computation
PROPOSAL: To scale up the flow-based computation of Wasserstein-2 barycentres to high-dimensional complex marginals, we introduce a hierarchical multi-level solver that parallelises OT maps computation across different levels of coarsening on the tree. Our Hierarchical MOT solver employs stratified averaging to share knowledge between hierarchically related OT maps, accelerating computation.
CONTROLS: We evaluate Hierarchical MOT against our previous Flow-IMF* solver, the iterative fixed-point barycentre computation, and the state-of-the-art neural parameterisation methods. We vary parameters such as the number of hierarchical levels, averaging strategies, and entropic regularisation to assess performance. For relevance, experiments include multi-marginal problems in 100-dimensional spaces.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This architecture is expected to significantly accelerate stable firstly barycentre computation, enabling calculations on higher-dimensional real-world datasets. Despite a large number of required GPU-hrs, Hierarchical Mot is predicted to achieve reductions in the computation time up to 6–10 times compared to the first solver.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Wasserstein-2 Barycentre Computation via Neural ODE Backpropagation
PROPOSAL: To enhance the scalability of Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation and overcome the challenges associated with inductive bias in hierarchically constructed OT maps, we propose an orthogonal extension: tex discrete approximation scheme as the ODE solver for Wasserstein-2 barycentre computations. We expect that our novel discretisation strategy will handle complex marginals and instability originating from non-linearly OT mappings in hierarchical settings, assessing equivalency starting from densely supplied sets.
CONTROLS: We compare our upgraded approach to the original Wasserstein-2 barycentre method and other state-of-the-art parameterisation methods. For systematic evaluation, we shall set multiple adversarial values of the entropic regularisation hyperparameter and assure consistency with prior results for diverse induced network architectures.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to considerably improve the computation of Wasserstein-2 barycentres by absorbing non-linear irregularities caused by the optimisation processes inherent in hierarchical OT mapping architectures, enabling application to highly-dense hierarchical networks.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Hierarchical MOT: A Multi-Level Flow-Based OT Solver for Scalable Barycentre Computation
PROPOSAL: To improve the performance and efficiency of Hierarchical MOT, we incorporate a self-correcting strategy based on the output of the Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation via neural ODE backpropagation, recently introduced and evaluated in our research. This approach, dubbed Hierarchical MOT*, aims to correct the strata-averaging approximation used across the levels by aligning the hierarchies of OT maps produced by both methods.
CONTROLS: We compare Hierarchical MOT* against its predecessor, the Flow-IMF* solver, and assess integration of this technique on high-dimensional barycentres which are harder to obtain solution-wise. We further investigate implications for instance learning Bayesian posterior aggregation tasks as recent evaluations show latter approached towards classifier accurately than control.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This self-correcting enhancement on Hierarchical Mot-style barycentre computation is expected to produce improved, accurate results with reduced errors for significantly higher dimensional complex distributions, initiated self-correcting role playing when effectively hierarchically members aligned are generated across all sets & the training dimensionality/utilisation gets boosted as required.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Scalability Assessment and Depth Selection for Hierarchical MOT
PROPOSAL: As hierarchical structures become increasingly complex, we investigate the scalability of Hierarchical MOT* and assess the impact of varying the number of hierarchy levels and depth selection on the efficiency and accuracy of Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation. This research seeks to identify an optimal hierarchy structure for Hierarchical MOT*, enabling explicit guidance on system design.
CONTROLS: We conduct a thorough study comparing the performance of Hierarchical MOT* across different hierarchy levels (2, 3, 4, and 5) and assess the effect of varying depth selection (injection) strategies on the OT maps computation. For fair comparison, we compare the accuracy and efficiency of the selected systems against the Flow-IMF* baseline and Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation methods.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Hierarchical MOT*, one approach to scalable barycentres, is predicted to be affected most positively when depth corresponds  upward to certain logic presented regarding branches akin distribution \(p_2\).

propositions.prediction: Flow-IMF** is expected to overcome the performance limitations faced by the original adaptation, showcasing consistent and fast convergence with real-world applications of Wasserstein-2 barycentres. Special emphasis is placed on performance in scenarios with low entropic regularisation, with Flow-IMF** demonstrating greater resilience.
propositions.texte: To refine our previous extension incorporating a convergence-preserving fixed-point iteration with overlapping sweeps, dubbed "Flow-IMF*," we now include an estimated Schrödinger bridge loss as an additional stabilising term in the solver's objective function. This novel Adaptation of Flow-IMF*, dubbed "Flow-IMF**," exploits the benefits of both fixed-point and probabilistic modelling schemes, merging the convergence properties of the former and the stability benefits of the latter.
propositions.titre: Efficient Fast Convergence for Tree-Structured Schrödinger Bridge

propositions.controles: We compare our upgraded approach to the original Wasserstein-2 barycentre method and other state-of-the-art parameterisation methods. For systematic evaluation, we shall set multiple adversarial values of the entropic regularisation hyperparameter and assure consistency with prior results for diverse induced network architectures.
propositions.prediction: This approach is expected to considerably improve the computation of Wasserstein-2 barycentres by absorbing non-linear irregularities caused by the optimisation processes inherent in hierarchical OT mapping architectures, enabling application to highly-dense hierarchical networks.
propositions.texte: To enhance the scalability of Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation and overcome the challenges associated with inductive bias in hierarchically constructed OT maps, we propose an orthogonal extension: tex discrete approximation scheme as the ODE solver for Wasserstein-2 barycentre computations. We expect that our novel discretisation strategy will handle complex marginals and instability originating from non-linearly OT mappings in hierarchical settings, assessing equivalency starting from densely supplied sets.
propositions.titre: Wasserstein-2 Barycentre Computation via Neural ODE Backpropagation

propositions.controles: We compare Hierarchical MOT* against its predecessor, the Flow-IMF* solver, and assess integration of this technique on high-dimensional barycentres which are harder to obtain solution-wise. We further investigate implications for instance learning Bayesian posterior aggregation tasks as recent evaluations show latter approached towards classifier accurately than control.
propositions.prediction: This self-correcting enhancement on Hierarchical Mot-style barycentre computation is expected to produce improved, accurate results with reduced errors for significantly higher dimensional complex distributions, initiated self-correcting role playing when effectively hierarchically members aligned are generated across all sets & the training dimensionality/utilisation gets boosted as required.
propositions.texte: To improve the performance and efficiency of Hierarchical MOT, we incorporate a self-correcting strategy based on the output of the Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation via neural ODE backpropagation, recently introduced and evaluated in our research. This approach, dubbed Hierarchical MOT*, aims to correct the strata-averaging approximation used across the levels by aligning the hierarchies of OT maps produced by both methods.
propositions.titre: Hierarchical MOT: A Multi-Level Flow-Based OT Solver for Scalable Barycentre Computation

propositions.controles: We conduct a thorough study comparing the performance of Hierarchical MOT* across different hierarchy levels (2, 3, 4, and 5) and assess the effect of varying depth selection (injection) strategies on the OT maps computation. For fair comparison, we compare the accuracy and efficiency of the selected systems against the Flow-IMF* baseline and Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation methods.
propositions.prediction: The Hierarchical MOT*, one approach to scalable barycentres, is predicted to be affected most positively when depth corresponds  upward to certain logic presented regarding branches akin distribution \(p_2\).
propositions.texte: As hierarchical structures become increasingly complex, we investigate the scalability of Hierarchical MOT* and assess the impact of varying the number of hierarchy levels and depth selection on the efficiency and accuracy of Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation. This research seeks to identify an optimal hierarchy structure for Hierarchical MOT*, enabling explicit guidance on system design.
propositions.titre: Scalability Assessment and Depth Selection for Hierarchical MOT
