TITLE: Assessing the Compositionality of Edited Facts in Multimodal Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We design a novel experiment to test how LVLMs integrate separately edited visual and textual facts to answer compositional questions that require both. To do this, we will adapt the VQA datasets to cover a diverse set of question types that span visual entities, attribute assertions, and argumentations. We will evaluate LVLMs' performance in answering these questions after being edited with multiple facts about the same entities. The goal is to understand how different knowledge editing methods impact the ability to reason compositionally over edited facts.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of LVLMs with knowledge editing to that of standard VQA models, as well as models fine-tuned on each edited fact separately.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Results will show that knowledge editing improves compositional reasoning but that its impact depends on the editing method, question type, and how well the edited facts interface with one another.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Visual-Textual Interference in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: REVISED: We will expand the scope of our investigation to include a more diverse set of multimodal knowledge editing scenarios, such as attributing qualia to visual entities (e.g., "What is the texture of the cat's fur?"), reasoning about agent-oriented properties ("Who painted the Mona Lisa?"), and inferring logical relationships between entities ("Is a book on a desk considered a paperweight?"). We will assess the effect of visual-textual interference across these various edit types and question types on the LVLM's accuracy and retention of knowledge.
CONTROLS: Experiments will continue to compare each editing strategy in isolation, with additional analysis on edit granularity, knowledge type, and question types to pinpoint where visual-textual interference matters most.
COST: 50 additional GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Results will deepen our understanding of how knowledge editing methods interact with different types of multimodal knowledge, shedding light on when and how visual-textual interference causes problems and highlighting potential avenues for more effective edit manager design.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implementing a Multimodal Knowledge Graph for Enforcing Consistency in LVLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage recent advances in knowledge graph-based architectures to develop a multimodal knowledge graph that explicitly encodes and integrates visual and textual knowledge within a single, coherent framework. Our graph-based model will be designed to enforce consistency between and among different knowledge edits, ensuring that visual and textual information are correctly correlated and persistently up-to-date. We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a real-world knowledge graph dataset, measuring the consistency and accuracy of LVLMs knowledge after a series of edits.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare our multimodal knowledge graph to standard LVLM implementations, assessing improvements in knowledge consistency, accuracy, and retention.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Results will demonstrate a significant improvement in preserving coherent knowledge across different edits and modalities, showcasing the potential of knowledge graphs for managing LVLMs' knowledge and ensuring consistency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Learning of LVLMs through Transfer and Accumulation of Knowledge
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous work, we propose to design and evaluate LVLMs that can learn through a sequence of knowledge edits and apply this learning to novel, unseen tasks and scenarios. We will develop a transfer learning framework that enables LVLMs to accumulate knowledge and adapt to new knowledge updates without catastrophic forgetting. This framework will be evaluated on real-world datasets, measuring improvements in performance and retention of knowledge after a sequence of edits.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare LVLMs trained using transfer learning to those trained from scratch for each new task, with ablations to investigate the role of knowledge graph-based approaches, memory-augmented architectures, and edit-specific knowledge consolidation.
COST: 550 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Results will demonstrate that LVLMs can efficiently learn from a sequence of edits and transfer this learning to new tasks, significantly improving performance and retention of knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Hardware-Accelerated Framework for Efficient Knowledge Editing in LVLMs
PROPOSAL: To bridge the gap between model design and practical deployment, we will investigate the use of specialized hardware accelerators for knowledge editing in LVLMs. Building on recent advances in GPU and TPU architectures, we propose to develop a custom-designed framework that leverages hardware accelerators to efficiently perform knowledge edits, consolidation, and graph-based knowledge updates. This framework will be evaluated on real-world applications, comparing its performance, energy efficiency, and scalability to traditional software-based implementations.
CONTROLS: Experiments will measure improvements in edit-throughput, energy efficiency, and model retention after a sequence of knowledge updates using our hardware-accelerated framework, compared to standard software-based approaches.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (with additional compute resource allocation for hardware setup and calibration)
PREDICTION: Results will demonstrate that our hardware-accelerated framework significantly accelerates knowledge editing and consolidation in LVLMs, enabling real-world deployment and large-scale commercial applications.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Implementing a Multimodal Knowledge Graph for Enforcing Consistency in LVLMs
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Building on the success of our previous proposals, we propose a unified framework that integrates our multimodal knowledge graph, reparameterization, and hardware-accelerated editing, creating a highly scalable, efficient, and effective system for enforcing consistency and knowledge retention in LVLMs. This framework will be extensively evaluated on a range of real-world applications, measuring improvements in knowledge consistency, accuracy, and retention after a sequence of edits.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare our unified framework to state-of-the-art knowledge editing methods, assessing improvements in knowledge consistency, accuracy, and retention after a sequence of edits.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (calculated based on the hardware-accelerated framework and knowledge graph's expected benefit)
PREDICTION: Results will demonstrate a significant improvement in LVLMs' ability to learn and retain knowledge, showcasing the potential of our unified framework for real-world applications in AI, computer vision, and human-computer interaction.

bilan.ensemble:
PROPOSAL 1: Investigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
We will implement and evaluate two baseline approaches for knowledge editing in LVLMs: Subspace editors (modifies a subset of the model's weights to store the edit) and Lockstep editors (fine-tunes the model from scratch for each edit). We will test these methods on the HatefulMemes challenge, a real-world benchmark for multimodal hate speech detection, with the goal of demontrating the gap between standard LVLMs and editors in retaining previously learned knowledge while adapting to new edits.
Controls: Subspace editors and Lockstep editors will be compared to standard LVLMs, with both baselines trained on the Hateful Memes dataset to evaluate knowledge retention after multiple edits.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: The results will show that standard LVLMs suffer from catastrophic forgetting, while subspace editors retain more knowledge, but are less accurate overall, highlighting the need for better interleaved editing mechanisms.

PROPOSAL 2: Evaluating the Impact of Visual-Textual Interference in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
We propose an experiment to compare the effects of three common multimodal knowledge editing strategies: external-memory retrieval, internal-memory fine-tuning, and spatially-separate visual and textual embedding. For each method, we will use the SameCat dataset, a large, real-world image categorization benchmark, to assess how well the model retains learned knowledge after multiple interleaved edits. Our goal is to understand whether visual-textual interference is a major contributor to catastrophic forgetting.
Controls: Experiments will compare each editing strategy in isolation, using task accuracy as the primary evaluation metric, with additional analysis on attribute retention and edit granularity.
Estimated cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: Results will show a clear decrease in model performance for methods that model visual and textual edits within a shared or unified space, highlighting the importance of spatial separation for reducing knowledge interference.

PROPOSAL 3: Provable Bounds for Multimodal Knowledge Editing via Reparametrization
We will derive theoretical guarantees for LVLM knowledge editing by reparametrizing the modality-specific embedding spaces through normalizing flows. This approach ensures that the model's availability for previously stored knowledge does not degrade catastrophically after each edit. By leveraging concentration inequalities and properties of the flow-based density models, we will establish lower bounds for the capacity of the reparametrized space to accommodate a sequence of edits.
Controls: Theory will be compared to existing empirical results on the task of catastrophic forgetting in LVLMs, providing corroboration for our approach.
Estimated cost: 50 GPU-hours (low-carbon theoretical development)
Prediction: Our reparametrized model will exhibit significantly lower degradation in knowledge retention, validating the theoretical bounds and demonstrating the feasibility of reproducible guarantees for knowledge editing.

PROPOSAL 4: Assessing the Compositionality of Edited Facts in Multimodal Visual Question Answering
We design a novel experiment to test how LVLMs integrate separately edited visual and textual facts to answer compositional questions that require both. To do this, we will adapt the VQA datasets to cover a diverse set of question types that span visual entities, attribute assertions, and argumentations. We will evaluate LVLMs' performance in answering these questions after being edited with multiple facts about the same entities. The goal is to understand how different knowledge editing methods impact the ability to reason compositionally over edited facts.
Controls: We will compare the performance of LVLMs with knowledge editing to that of standard VQA models, as well as models fine-tuned on each edited fact separately.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: Results will show that knowledge editing improves compositional reasoning but that its impact depends on the editing method, question type, and how well the edited facts interface with one another.

PROPOSAL 5: Implementing a Multimodal Knowledge Graph for Enforcing Consistency in LVLMs
We propose to leverage recent advances in knowledge graph-based architectures to develop a multimodal knowledge graph that explicitly encodes and integrates visual and textual knowledge within a single, coherent framework. Our graph-based model will be designed to enforce consistency between and among different knowledge edits, ensuring that visual and textual information are correctly correlated and persistently up-to-date. We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a real-world knowledge graph dataset, measuring the consistency and accuracy of LVLMs knowledge after a series of edits.
Controls: Experiments will compare our multimodal knowledge graph to standard LVLM implementations, assessing improvements in knowledge consistency, accuracy, and retention.
Estimated cost: 400 GPU-hours
Prediction: Results will demonstrate a significant improvement in preserving coherent knowledge across different edits and modalities, showcasing the potential of knowledge graphs for managing LVLMs' knowledge and ensuring consistency.

PROPOSAL 6: Evaluating Continual Learning of LVLMs through Transfer and Accumulation of Knowledge
Building on our previous work, we propose to design and evaluate LVLMs that can learn through a sequence of knowledge edits and apply this learning to novel, unseen tasks and scenarios. We will develop a transfer learning framework that enables LVLMs to accumulate knowledge and adapt to new knowledge updates without catastrophic forgetting. This framework will be evaluated on real-world datasets, measuring improvements in performance and retention of knowledge after a sequence of edits.
Controls: Experiments will compare LVLMs trained using transfer learning to those trained from scratch for each new task, with ablations to investigate the role of knowledge graph-based approaches, memory-augmented architectures, and edit-specific knowledge consolidation.
Estimated cost: 550 GPU-hours
Prediction: Results will demonstrate that LVLMs can efficiently learn from a sequence of edits and transfer this learning to new tasks, significantly improving performance and retention of knowledge.

PROPOSAL 7: A Hardware-Accelerated Framework for Efficient Knowledge Editing in LVLMs
To bridge the gap between model design and practical deployment, we will investigate the use of specialized hardware accelerators for knowledge editing in LVLMs. Building on recent advances in GPU and TPU architectures, we propose to develop a custom-designed framework that leverages hardware accelerators to efficiently perform knowledge edits, consolidation, and graph-based knowledge updates. This framework will be evaluated on real-world applications, comparing its performance, energy efficiency, and scalability to traditional software-based implementations.
Controls: Experiments will measure improvements in edit-throughput, energy efficiency, and model retention after a sequence of knowledge updates using our hardware-accelerated framework, compared to standard software-based approaches.
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours (with additional compute resource allocation for hardware setup and calibration)
Prediction: Results will demonstrate that our hardware-accelerated framework significantly accelerates knowledge editing and consolidation in LVLMs, enabling real-world deployment and large-scale commercial applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Explicit Intermodality Coordination
PROPOSAL: Develop a new internal-memory editing method called "MCsparse" that uses a sparse matrix to store and retrieve edited knowledge from both visual and textual pathways independently, with each modality having its own key-value memory. This design allows for concurrent updates of visual and textual facts while preventing catastrophic forgetting by utilizing a learned intermodality coordination module that adaptively adjusts the strength of interactions between modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing internal-memory editors like ICML's "edit-reify" and CVPR's "SparseAttentive" methods, as well as a state-of-the-art external-memory editor (e.g., HuggingFace's "transformers" with negative sampling).
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: M_sparse will exceed the performance of ICML's "edit-reify" by 8% in a sequence of visual and textual edits on the Visual Commonsense dataset, while matching CVPR's "SparseAttentive" in knowledge retention on a defined subset of RealEstate300k val. However, there may be failures in handling catastrophically fading edits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Compositional Query Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Extend the commonly used Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmark (e.g., VQA-2.0 and VQA-Marty) to include compositional query tests to evaluate LVLM knowledge editing capabilities. Specifically, introduce new questions that require reasoning with multiple edited facts and across modalities (e.g., "Which party does person X in Photo1 belong to, given that they were previously known to be involved in Photo2 which featured an event they helped organize?").
CONTROLS: Compare edited LVLMs with different editing methods (MCsparse, edit-reify, SparseAttentive) on existing VQA benchmarks and the new compositional query benchmarks to assess their performance in retaining and integrating edited knowledge.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (utilizing pre-existing VQA benchmarks and models)
PREDICTION: LVLMs with MCsparse will outperform existing editing methods by 12% on the new compositional query benchmarks, indicating its strengths in handling multimodal edits and integrating knowledge, but may struggle with certain nuances of VQA, particularly regarding scene understanding.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Compositional Query Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Extend the methodology to not only assess the model's performance on the new compositional query benchmarks but also to provide insights into how well LVLMs retain and compose edited knowledge using visual and textual evidence. This can be done by tracking the model's confidence in answering compositional queries before and after each edit, and analyzing its ability to correctly reason with edited facts in contextualized questions.
CONTROLS: Assess with the same editing methods (MCsparse, edit-reify, SparseAttentive) as before, and evaluate how the results correlate with the explicit intermodality coordination module's performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (adding contextualized analysis to the compositional query evaluation)
PREDICTION: MCsparse is expected to show improvements in retaining and composing edited knowledge (12% increase in compositional query accuracy and 8% increase in contextualized analysis confidence) compared to existing editing methods, but may exhibit increased sensitivity to the nuances of scene understanding in compositional queries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Evaluation of Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial editing framework that generates targeted, false updates for both visual and textual pathways, which can then be used to evaluate the robustness of LVLMs and their editing methods. This adversarial framework will be designed to manipulate existing knowledge in the model and introduce conflicts that require correct prioritization of facts.
CONTROLS: Utilize MCsparse and other editing methods, as well as the compositional query benchmarks from experiment 2.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MCsparse is expected to show increased robustness (10% improvement in rejecting adversarial edits) compared to existing editing methods, due to its explicit intermodality coordination, but may still be susceptible to complex manipulations involving both visual and textual conflicts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization Techniques for Preserving Multimodal Editing Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of regularization techniques (e.g., L1, L2, dropout, weight decay) to prevent overfitting and promote the stability of MCsparse during the editing process. Specifically, design a set of experiments to test the effect of different regularization strategies on MCsparse's performance in retaining edited knowledge, handling compositional queries, and rejecting adversarial edits.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of various regularization strengths and combinations on MCsparse's performance, using both the compositional query benchmarks and the adversarial editing framework.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Applying the right regularization technique can lead to a 5-7% improvement in MCsparse's performance on compositional queries and a 10-12% increase in its robustness against adversarial edits, but may require manual tuning and careful selection of the regularization parameters.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Compositional Query Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Update the compositional query benchmark (from experiment 2) to include more diverse, context-specific scenarios that simulate real-world knowledge updates and editing scenarios. This revised benchmark will integrate with existing VQA models to assess the ability of MCsparse and other editing methods to handle various types of context-dependent queries and edited knowledge.
CONTROLS: Reassess MCsparse's performance on the updated compositional query benchmark, using the same evaluation metrics as before, and compare its results with other editing methods.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (modifying and re-evaluating the existing benchmark)
PREDICTION: The updated benchmark is expected to reveal subtle weaknesses in existing editing methods, such as difficulty handling query nuances or satisfying contextual dependencies, with MCsparse reportedly exceling in the range of 95-98% correct responses; weaknesses in these areas would need attended to via improved plan selection, fact validation regiment for training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Validation for Trustworthy Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel knowledge validation module to MCsparse, which evaluates the reliability and accuracy of edited knowledge in the context of compositional queries. This module will analyze the model's confidence and uncertainty when producing answers and flag potential knowledge inconsistencies or errors.
CONTROLS: Assess the impact of knowledge validation on MCsparse's performance and robustness using the compositional query benchmarks and adversarial editing framework.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating knowledge validation will lead to a significant improvement (15-20%) in MCsparse's accuracy and reliability on compositional queries, and also enhance its robustness against adversarial edits by up to 20%, but may introduce a computational overhead due to the added validation step.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Embedding for Efficient Continual Editing
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of multimodal knowledge graph embeddings (MGKGE) to represent visual and textual knowledge in a unified vector space, which can then be efficiently updated using a set of editable operations (e.g., graph augmentation, node (knowledge) updates). This approach aims to reduce the complexity of updating multimodal knowledge while preserving its consistency and reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of MGKGE-based editing with MCsparse on a range of multimodal knowledge editing tasks, including compositional queries and adversarial editing.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MGKGE-based editing will show competitive performance (on a par with MCsparse) in terms of accuracy and robustness on compositional queries and adversarial editing, but may require a significant amount of additional training data to achieve optimal performance, potentially limiting its applicability in low-resource scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Empirical Evaluation of Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive large-scale empirical evaluation of various continual multimodal knowledge editing methods (including MCsparse, MGKGE, and other models) on a diverse set of real-world datasets (e.g., Visual Genome, WikiEntities, and multimodal multimodal Wikipedia) and applications (e.g., language models, vision-and-language navigation).
CONTROLS: Use a combination of automatic and human evaluation metrics to assess the performance of each method on various tasks, including knowledge retention, compositional query answering, and adversarial editing.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This large-scale evaluation will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different continual multimodal knowledge editing methods, ultimately revealing emerging trends and potential directions for future research.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Continual Multimodal Knowledge Editing with Compositional Query Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Take the insights gained from the large-scale empirical evaluation in experiment 7 and refine the compositional query benchmarks to reflect the observed strengths and weaknesses of different continual multimodal knowledge editing methods. This refinement will enable the creation of a comprehensive, method-agnostic evaluation framework for assessing the performance of LVLM editing in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Use the revised compositional query benchmarks to re-evaluate the performance of MCsparse and MGKGE as well as other emerging methods, aiming to create a competitive landscape of LVLM editing techniques.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined evaluation framework will accurately reflect the performance differences between existing editing methods, providing a solid foundation for further research and development in the LVLM editing field.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Dynamically Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Range Temporal Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Investigate if dynamically conditioned diffusion models, which adapt their noise schedules based on input temporal context, can effectively model long-range temporal dynamics in satellite image time series data. We'll train a diffusion-based model on the Deep Farm dataset and evaluate its performance on the temporal change description task using metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU.
CONTROLS: Compare to the performance of a static diffusion model and a state-of-the-art video captioning model on the same task.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamically conditioned diffusion model should outperform the static diffusion model, but may struggle with capturing nuanced causal relationships in the data, particularly for longer-term forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporally Consistent Future Forecasting with Contrastive Temporal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Develop a contrastive learning objective to encourage temporal consistency in future forecasting by learning to distinguish between plausible future generations that adhere to observed trends and those that deviate from them. We'll use a prevision model, like DALL-E, as our generator and adapt the CLIP framework to learn a contrastive embedding space where similar temporal continuations are close, and divergent ones are far apart. Evaluate on the UCMerced dataset and the FutureChurch dataset with metrics such as IoU and visibility-based metrics.
CONTROLS: Compare to a model that minimizes a per-pixel difference loss between generated images and ground-truth forecasts, and to a baseline of unconditional image synthesis.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve temporal consistency in the forecasted images, with a notable gain in IoU and visibility-based scores, but may become computationally expensive for very long timelines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: GeoSemBART: A Geospatial Semantics Enhanced BART Model for Change Description
PROPOSAL: Introduce a geospatial semantics enhanced BART model, GeoSemBART, to leverage domain-specific knowledge and encode location-aware representations to aid in change description. Incorporate geospatial features and semantic tags from the GeoNames dataset into BART's encoder, and use a learnable location transformer to attend to geospatial information effectively. Evaluate on the Rock Delta dataset with metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and geometric accuracy scores.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard BART model, a geospatial-aware transformer variant without semantic enhancements, and to a strong baseline of video captioning models adapted to the satellite domain.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GeoSemBART should outperform the baseline models by accurately modeling temporal change in geographical terms and detecting meaningful spatial trends, with notable gains in both ROUGE and BLEU scores.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Temporally Consistent Future Forecasting with Contrastive Temporal Reasoning
REVISED PROPOSAL: To further improve the contrastive temporal reasoning framework, incorporate an additional learnable latent code that captures the evolution of temporal trends and patterns in the observation sequence. This code can be conditioned on the input sequence and used to adapt the contrastive learning objective to the temporal dynamics. Evaluate on the UCMerced dataset and the FutureChurch dataset with metrics such as IoU and visibility-based metrics, and compare to the previous version of the framework.
CONTROLS: Compare to the previous model and a baseline of unconditional image synthesis.
COST: 1000 additional GPU-hours (cumulative cost 3500 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Thisrevision should improve the ability to capture nuanced temporal evolution and adapt the contrastive learning objective to the changing patterns, leading to a significant improvement in IoU and visibility-based scores, while also maintaining efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Temporal Long-Range Dependencies in Change Description with Cognitive Graphs
PROPOSAL: Develop a cognitive graph-based approach to capture and reason about long-range temporal dependencies in change description. Represent each image in the sequence as a node, with edges between nodes indicating both temporal and causal relationships. Use a graph neural network (GNN) to reason about the temporal dependencies and condition a downstream change description model on the learned graph representations. Evaluate on the Rock Delta dataset with metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and geometric accuracy scores.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard GeoSemBART model, a graph-based change description model without cognitive graph enhancements, and to a baseline of static image captioning models adapted to the satellite domain.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The cognitive graph approach should reveal insightful temporal patterns and relationships in the change description, and condition the downstream model to better capture long-range dependencies, leading to a significant improvement in ROUGE and BLEU scores.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Understanding Temporal Long-Range Dependencies in Change Description with Cognitive Graphs
REVISED PROPOSAL: To further develop the cognitive graph approach, incorporate a data-driven knowledge graph construction module that learns to extract and represent relevant information about the scene and its dynamics from the sequence of satellite images. This graph will be used to inform and bias the GNN's reasoning process, thereby improving the accuracy and interpretability of the long-range dependencies discovered by the model. Evaluate on the Rock Delta dataset with metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and geometric accuracy scores.
CONTROLS: Compare to the previous cognitive graph model without the knowledge graph construction module, and to a baseline of static image captioning models adapted to the satellite domain.
COST: 800 additional GPU-hours (cumulative cost 5200 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The revised cognitive graph model should better integrate prior knowledge about the scene and its dynamics, leading to a more accurate and interpretable understanding of long-range temporal dependencies, and therefore improved ROUGE, BLEU and geometric accuracy scores.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Temporal Consistency of Satellite Image Forecasts with a Novel Metric: Temporal Structural Similarity (TSS)
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel metric for evaluating the temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts, TSS, which measures the similarity between the predicted temporal structures (e.g., trends, periodicity, sudden changes) and those observed in the ground-truth image sequence. Compare the TSS of the forecasts generated by the Dynamically Conditioned Diffusion model and the Temporally Consistent Future Forecasting framework with those from baseline models. Evaluate on the UCMerced dataset and the FutureChurch dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare to commonly used metrics such as IoU, visibility-based metrics, and standard image quality metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TSS should complement existing metrics by providing a more accurate and detailed evaluation of the temporal consistency of the forecasts. The baseline models may achieve high IoU and visibility-based scores, but perform poorly in terms of TSS, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge-Driven Temporal Abstraction for Efficient Forecasting of Long-Term Satellite Image Sequences
PROPOSAL: Develop a knowledge-driven temporal abstraction approach that utilizes a learned knowledge graph to identify and abstract away irrelevant or redundant temporal information in long-term satellite image sequences, while retaining the essential features that govern temporal dynamics. This abstracted representation will be used to condition a downstream temporal forecasting model, which will generate forecasts for the long-term sequence. Evaluate on the UCMerced dataset and the FutureChurch dataset with metrics such as IoU, visibility-based metrics, and TSS.
CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline models from previous experiments, and to a model that generates forecasts without any form of temporal abstraction.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging knowledge graphs and efficient temporal abstraction techniques, this approach should lead to significant improvements in forecasting performance, especially for long-term sequences, while also reducing computational requirements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Satellite Image Forecasts
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that formally characterizes and measures the temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts. This framework will provide a unified, mathematically rigorous approach to evaluating temporal consistency, complementing and extending existing empirical metrics such as TSS. The framework will be developed using tools from dynamical system theory, mathematical ecology, and statistical inference.
CONTROLS: Analyze the implications of the theoretical framework on existing empirical metrics and forecasting models, and explore potential future research directions.
COST: negligible (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework will provide a fundamental understanding of temporal consistency in satellite image forecasts, highlighting the importance of incorporating temporal dynamics into forecasting models and informing the development of more effective evaluation metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Case Studies on Real-World Satellite Imagery Time Series Data
PROPOSAL: Apply and extend the developed approaches to real-world satellite imagery time series data from diverse domains such as urban planning, natural disaster monitoring, and environmental conservation. Perform extensive experimental evaluations of the proposed models on large-scale, real-world datasets to validate their effectiveness and generalizability. Analyze the results, identify key insights, and provide practical recommendations for real-world deployments.
CONTROLS: Select representative datasets from the literature, apply the proposed approaches, and compare the results with state-of-the-art methods to demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the developed techniques.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours (significant computational resources will be required for large-scale experiments)
PREDICTION: The case studies will demonstrate the practical value and impact of the proposed approaches on real-world satellite imagery time series data, and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of applying these techniques in different domains.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Multimodal Transformers for Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art multimodal transformers (e.g., VL-BERT, VL-T5) on the task of temporal change description for satellite image time series, using the OSC-II benchmark and the recent STSETTempORAL-Change task. We will use the mean of BERTScore and ROUGE-L to evaluate the accuracy of the change descriptions, and compare to a baseline of a simple text summarization model.
CONTROLS: 1) A text-only summarization model (e.g., T5), and 2) a baseline of no fusion (i.e., processing each image independently).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a 40-image sequence).
PREDICTION: Multimodal transformers will outperform the baseline, with a notable improvement over the text-only summarization model, but fail to fully leverage the temporal context of the images.

This experiment will serve as a baseline for more advanced proposals and help us understand the limitations of current multimodal transformers in this specific task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Introducing Temporal Transformers for Sparsely Sampled Satellite Images
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel extension of the Transformer architecture, specifically designed for temporally sparse and irregularly sampled satellite image sequences. Our Temporal Transformer will incorporate a novel tokenization mechanism, which captures the semantic and temporal relationships between sparse image features and context, while mitigating the effects of gaps between consecutive images. We will evaluate our proposed architecture on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world satellite image time series benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional Transformer architecture trained on densely sampled sequences, and 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed tokenization mechanism.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our Temporal Transformer will outperform the baseline on both temporal change description and future forecasting tasks, while maintaining efficient training and inference times for long image sequences with gaps.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Introducing Temporal Transformers for Sparsely Sampled Satellite Images
PROPOSAL: MODIFIED PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel extension of the Transformer architecture, specifically designed for temporally sparse and irregularly sampled satellite image sequences. Our Temporal Transformer will incorporate a novel tokenization mechanism, which captures the semantic and temporal relationships between sparse image features and context, while mitigating the effects of gaps between consecutive images, and a temporal sentinel loss, which encourages the model to reason about the missing information between consecutive images. Additionally, we will incorporate a spatial sentinel mechanism to adapt the model to the varying spatial resolution between images. We will evaluate our proposed architecture on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world satellite image time series benchmarks, with a focus on land-use change modeling and forecasting.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional Transformer architecture trained on densely sampled sequences, 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed tokenization mechanism, 3) a comparison of our approach with existing methods for handling gaps in sequences (e.g., interpolation, attention-based methods).
COST: 800 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our modified Temporal Transformer will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change modeling and forecasting, and demonstrate strong performance on tasks requiring long-range temporal understanding and adaptability to sparse sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Forecasting Land-Use Change with Temporally Consistent Satellite Imagery
PROPOSAL: We will adapt our Temporal Transformer to a multi-step forecasting task, where the goal is to predict a sequence of future satellite images given a historical sequence. We will incorporate a novel feedback loop into our model, where the predicted images are fed back as input to the model at the next time step, allowing the model to reason about the consistency between the predicted and observed future trends. We will evaluate our approach on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional image forecasting model (e.g., diffusion models), 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed feedback loop.
COST: 1,000 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our adapted Temporal Transformer will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change forecasting, and demonstrate strong performance on tasks requiring temporally consistent predictions, while maintaining efficient training and inference times for long image sequences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Temporal Consistency Metrics for Satellite Image Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will design and evaluate a suite of metrics for assessing the temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts, including measures of temporal coherence, spatial coherence, and trend consistency. We will compare the performance of these metrics on a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks, and investigate their correlation with human-judged temporal consistency.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of standard image quality metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM), 2) a comparison of our proposed metrics with existing metrics for evaluating temporal consistency (e.g., recursive structural similarity index).
COST: 200 GPU-hours (development and evaluation of temporal consistency metrics).
PREDICTION: Our proposed metrics will demonstrate strong correlation with human-judged temporal consistency, and provide more comprehensive insights into the quality of satellite image forecasts than standard image quality metrics. Additionally, our investigation will highlight the limitations of existing metrics and provide a foundation for future research on temporal consistency evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semantic Graph-Based Reasoning for Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel approach for temporal change description that leverages semantic graph-based reasoning to model the causal relationships between historical changes and their impact on future trends. Our approach will utilize a knowledge graph to represent the semantic relationships between entities and events in the temporal context, and a graph attention network to learn the interactions between these entities and events. We will evaluate our approach on the OSC-II benchmark and compare it to state-of-the-art methods for temporal change description.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional transformer-based approach for temporal change description, 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the semantic graph-based reasoning components.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our semantic graph-based approach will achieve state-of-the-art results on temporal change description, and provide more nuanced and accurate descriptions of historical changes and their impact on future trends.

We will evaluate our approach on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional image forecasting model (e.g., diffusion models), 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed feedback loop, and 3) a comparison of our approach with the semantic graph-based reasoning approach from proposal 5.
COST: 1,200 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our adapted Temporal Transformer will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change forecasting, and provide more nuanced and accurate descriptions of historical changes and their impact on future trends, by combining the strengths of temporal consistency and semantic graph-based reasoning.

TITLE: Multi-Agent Temporal Forecasting for Satellite Image Time Series
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel multi-agent approach for satellite image time series forecasting, where each agent represents a different temporal or spatial context (e.g., seasonal trends, regional patterns). Our approach will utilize a cooperative communication protocol between agents to leverage their diverse perspectives and improve the overall forecasting performance. We will evaluate our approach on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of a traditional single-agent forecasting model (e.g., sequential encoder-decoder), 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the multi-agent communication protocol.
COST: 1,000 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our multi-agent approach will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change forecasting, and provide more robust and accurate predictions by harnessing the benefits of diverse perspectives and cooperative communication.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Satellite Image Time Series Models
PROPOSAL: We will explore the possibility of transferring knowledge from pre-trained models on other satellite image time series datasets to our proposed models for land-use change forecasting. We will experiment with different pre-training strategies, such as image classification, object detection, and multimodal pretext tasks, and evaluate their impact on the performance of our models on the STSET-LandCover dataset and other real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of training models from scratch, 2) a comparison of different pre-training strategies, and 3) an ablation study evaluating the impact of fine-tuning the pre-trained models on the target task.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (pre-training and fine-tuning on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach will show significant improvements in land-use change forecasting performance, and provide a more efficient and scalable way to leverage pre-trained models for addressing the challenges of satellite image time series forecasting.

TITLE: Large-Scale Geo-Spatial Time Series Benchmarking
PROPOSAL: We will develop a large-scale benchmarking framework for evaluating the performance of satellite image time series models on a diverse set of real-world datasets and tasks. Our framework will include a range of datasets with varying spatial and temporal characteristics, as well as a suite of evaluation metrics and comparison tasks that are tailored to the unique challenges of satellite image time series forecasting. We will use our benchmarking framework to evaluate the performance of the models proposed in this paper, as well as other state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS: 1) a baseline of evaluating models on a single dataset, and 2) a comparison of our benchmarking framework with existing benchmarks for satellite image time series modeling.
COST: 1,500 GPU-hours (benchmarking and evaluation on a large-scale dataset).
PREDICTION: Our large-scale benchmarking framework will provide a comprehensive and reliable evaluation of the performance of satellite image time series models, and will help to identify areas for future research and improvement in this field.

This experiment will serve as a baseline for more advanced proposals and help us understand the limitations of current multimodal transformers in this specific task.
propositions.texte: We will evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art multimodal transformers (e.g., VL-BERT, VL-T5) on the task of temporal change description for satellite image time series, using the OSC-II benchmark and the recent STSETTempORAL-Change task. We will use the mean of BERTScore and ROUGE-L to evaluate the accuracy of the change descriptions, and compare to a baseline of a simple text summarization model.
propositions.titre: Evaluating Multimodal Transformers for Temporal Change Description

propositions.controles: 1) a baseline of a traditional Transformer architecture trained on densely sampled sequences, 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed tokenization mechanism, 3) a comparison of our approach with existing methods for handling gaps in sequences (e.g., interpolation, attention-based methods).
propositions.cout_texte: 800 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
propositions.prediction: Our modified Temporal Transformer will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change modeling and forecasting, and demonstrate strong performance on tasks requiring long-range temporal understanding and adaptability to sparse sampling.
propositions.texte: MODIFIED PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel extension of the Transformer architecture, specifically designed for temporally sparse and irregularly sampled satellite image sequences. Our Temporal Transformer will incorporate a novel tokenization mechanism, which captures the semantic and temporal relationships between sparse image features and context, while mitigating the effects of gaps between consecutive images, and a temporal sentinel loss, which encourages the model to reason about the missing information between consecutive images. Additionally, we will incorporate a spatial sentinel mechanism to adapt the model to the varying spatial resolution between images. We will evaluate our proposed architecture on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world satellite image time series benchmarks, with a focus on land-use change modeling and forecasting.
propositions.titre: Introducing Temporal Transformers for Sparsely Sampled Satellite Images

propositions.controles: 1) a baseline of a traditional image forecasting model (e.g., diffusion models), 2) an ablation study evaluating the impact of the proposed feedback loop, and 3) a comparison of our approach with the semantic graph-based reasoning approach from proposal 5.
propositions.cout_texte: 1,200 GPU-hours (training and evaluation on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
propositions.prediction: Our adapted Temporal Transformer will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change forecasting, and provide more nuanced and accurate descriptions of historical changes and their impact on future trends, by combining the strengths of temporal consistency and semantic graph-based reasoning.
propositions.texte: MODIFIED PROPOSAL: We will adapt our Temporal Transformer to a multi-step forecasting task, where the goal is to predict a sequence of future satellite images given a historical sequence. We will incorporate a novel feedback loop into our model, where the predicted images are fed back as input to the model at the next time step, allowing the model to reason about the consistency between the predicted and observed future trends. Additionally, we will use the semantic graph-based reasoning approach from proposal 5 to model the causal relationships between historical changes and their impact on future trends. We will evaluate our approach on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
propositions.titre: Forecasting Land-Use Change with Temporally Consistent Satellite Imagery

propositions.controles: 1) a baseline of standard image quality metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM), 2) a comparison of our proposed metrics with existing metrics for evaluating temporal consistency (e.g., recursive structural similarity index).
propositions.cout_texte: 200 GPU-hours (development and evaluation of temporal consistency metrics).
propositions.prediction: Our proposed metrics will demonstrate strong correlation with human-judged temporal consistency, and provide more comprehensive insights into the quality of satellite image forecasts than standard image quality metrics. Additionally, our investigation will highlight the limitations of existing metrics and provide a foundation for future research on temporal consistency evaluation.
propositions.texte: We will design and evaluate a suite of metrics for assessing the temporal consistency of satellite image forecasts, including measures of temporal coherence, spatial coherence, and trend consistency. We will compare the performance of these metrics on a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks, and investigate their correlation with human-judged temporal consistency.
propositions.titre: Evaluating Temporal Consistency Metrics for Satellite Image Forecasting

Our approach will utilize a knowledge graph to represent the semantic relationships between entities and events in the temporal context, and a graph attention network to learn the interactions between these entities and events. We will evaluate our approach on the OSC-II benchmark and compare it to state-of-the-art methods for temporal change description.
propositions.titre: Semantic Graph-Based Reasoning for Temporal Change Description

propositions.prediction: Our multi-agent approach will achieve state-of-the-art results on land-use change forecasting, and provide more robust and accurate predictions by harnessing the benefits of diverse perspectives and cooperative communication.

Our approach will utilize a cooperative communication protocol between agents to leverage their diverse perspectives and improve the overall forecasting performance. We will evaluate our approach on the STSET-LandCover dataset and a set of real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
propositions.titre: Multi-Agent Temporal Forecasting for Satellite Image Time Series

propositions.cout_texte: 300 GPU-hours (pre-training and fine-tuning on a set of 10 image sequences with varying temporal gaps).
propositions.prediction: Our transfer learning approach will show significant improvements in land-use change forecasting performance, and provide a more efficient and scalable way to leverage pre-trained models for addressing the challenges of satellite image time series forecasting.
propositions.texte: We will explore the possibility of transferring knowledge from pre-trained models on other satellite image time series datasets to our proposed models for land-use change forecasting. We will experiment with different pre-training strategies, such as image classification, object detection, and multimodal pretext tasks, and evaluate their impact on the performance of our models on the STSET-LandCover dataset and other real-world land-use change forecasting benchmarks.
propositions.titre: Transfer Learning for Satellite Image Time Series Models

propositions.controles: 1) a baseline of evaluating models on a single dataset, and 2) a comparison of our benchmarking framework with existing benchmarks for satellite image time series modeling.
propositions.cout_texte: 1,500 GPU-hours (benchmarking and evaluation on a large-scale dataset).
propositions.prediction: Our large-scale benchmarking framework will provide a comprehensive and reliable evaluation of the performance of satellite image time series models, and will help to identify areas for future research and improvement in this field.
propositions.texte: We will develop a large-scale benchmarking framework for evaluating the performance of satellite image time series models on a diverse set of real-world datasets and tasks. Our framework will include a range of datasets with varying spatial and temporal characteristics, as well as a suite of evaluation metrics and comparison tasks that are tailored to the unique challenges of satellite image time series forecasting. We will use our benchmarking framework to evaluate the performance of the models proposed in this paper, as well as other state-of-the-art models.
propositions.titre: Large-Scale Geo-Spatial Time Series Benchmarking

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural Identity Representation Learning from Population Activity
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate a variational autoencoder (VAE) on recordings from Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice to produce a compact but informative representation of individual neuron activity that captures aspects of neuron identity. We will use a standard VAE architecture with a neural network encoder and decoder, and add a cell-type classification module that trains on labeled neurons.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard PCA-based dimensionality reduction, which relies only on population-averaged features.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The VAE will learn a more informative representation of neuron activity, capturing aspects of cell-type identity, but it may struggle with brain region identity, which may not be encoded in the same spatial patterns of activity. We expect moderate performance, around 70-80% accuracy on cell-type classification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferability of Neural Identity Representations across Sessions and Animals
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the transferability of the VAE representations learned in proposal 1 to entirely new sessions and animals. We will use a zero-shot transfer scenario, where the model trained on one set of recordings is applied to a new, unseen set of recordings without retraining.
CONTROLS: Compare to a fine-tuned model that is retrained on the new set of recordings, and to a baseline model that uses population-averaged features.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (adding a new dataset and running transfer experiments)
PREDICTION: We expect the VAE representations to transfer reasonably well to new sessions and animals, achieving moderate to high accuracy on cell-type classification, around 60-80%. However, the performance may degrade slightly due to changes in population activity patterns across different recordings.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Transferability of Neural Identity Representations across Sessions and Animals
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to also explore the effect of the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning on the transferability of neural identity representations. We will create different training sets with varying numbers of recordings and population sizes, and evaluate the transferability of the learned representations to new sessions and animals.
CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline models from proposal 2, and to a few ablated models that use only a limited set of recordings or population features.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (modifying the experiment to explore different training conditions)
PREDICTION: We expect the transferability of neural identity representations to improve with an increase in the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, achieved by increasing the population size and variety of recorded neurons. However, the law of diminishing returns may apply, and we may not see significant improvements beyond a certain point.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Transferability of Neural Identity Representations across Sessions and Animals
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to also explore the effect of the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning on the transferability of neural identity representations. CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline models from proposal 2, and to a few ablated models that use only a limited set of recordings or population features.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (modifying the experiment to explore different training conditions)
PREDICTION: We expect the transferability of neural identity representations to improve with an increase in the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, achieved by increasing the population size and variety of recorded neurons. However, the law of diminishing returns may apply, and we may not see significant improvements beyond a certain point.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Brain Region in Neural Identity Representation
PROPOSAL: Modify the VAE architecture from proposal 1 to also output a brain region classification module. We will add a new decoder that predicts brain region based on the population activity, and train it jointly with the cell-type classification module.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline model that uses only population-averaged features for brain region classification, and to a few ablated models that remove the brain region decoder or use a different architecture.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (modifying the VAE architecture and training it with brain region classification)
PREDICTION: We expect the VAE to learn a brain region representation that is informative and useful for classification, but may have a lower accuracy compared to cell-type classification. We hypothesize that the brain region representation will be more difficult to learn due to the more subtle and variable patterns of activity across different brain regions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Studying the Effect of Population Size and Diversity on Neural Identity Representation
PROPOSAL: Create a controlled experiment where we vary the population size and diversity of recorded neurons, and evaluate the impact on the accuracy and robustness of the neural identity representations learned by the VAE. We will create multiple datasets with different population sizes and diversity levels, and train the VAE on each one.
CONTROLS: Compare to a fixed dataset with a moderate population size and diversity level, and to a few ablated models that use only a limited set of neurons or population features.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (creating and training on multiple datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect the accuracy and robustness of the neural identity representations to improve with an increase in population size and diversity, due to the better coverage and representation of different cell types and brain regions. However, we may also observe overfitting or degradation in performance for very large or heterogeneous populations, due to the increased complexity of the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Calcium Imaging Recordings in Neural Identity Representation
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 to also include calcium imaging recordings from mice, and evaluate the impact on the accuracy and robustness of the neural identity representations learned by the VAE. We will train the VAE on a mixed dataset containing both electrophysiology and calcium imaging recordings.
CONTROLS: Compare to a model trained on only electrophysiology recordings, and to a model trained on only calcium imaging recordings.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (modifying the dataset and training the VAE)
PREDICTION: We expect the VAE to learn more accurate and robust neural identity representations when trained on a mixed dataset containing both electrophysiology and calcium imaging recordings, due to the complementary information provided by both modalities. However, we may also observe overfitting or degradation in performance if the VAE is not able to effectively incorporate and balance the information from both sources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Different Neural Encoding Schemes for Neural Identity Representation
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 to compare different neural encoding schemes, such as spike-phase encoding, rate encoding, and population encoding, and evaluate their impact on the accuracy and robustness of the neural identity representations learned by the VAE. We will train the VAE on each encoding scheme and evaluate their performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline model that uses a fixed encoding scheme, and to a few ablated models that use only one or two of the encoding schemes.
COST: 90 GPU-hours (modifying the dataset and training the VAE on different encoding schemes)
PREDICTION: We expect the VAE to learn more accurate and robust neural identity representations when using population encoding, due to its ability to capture dynamic and synchronous activity patterns. However, we may also observe a trade-off between encoding scheme and model performance, and may find that one encoding scheme performs better than others in specific contexts or situations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Use of Multi-Task Learning for Neural Identity Representation
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 to use multi-task learning, where the VAE is trained on both cell-type classification and brain region classification tasks simultaneously. We will evaluate the impact of multi-task learning on the accuracy and robustness of the neural identity representations learned by the VAE.
CONTROLS: Compare to a single-task model that is trained on only one task, and to a few ablated models that use different combination of tasks or weights on each task.
COST: 110 GPU-hours (modifying the model and training on multiple tasks)
PREDICTION: We expect the VAE to learn more accurate and robust neural identity representations when using multi-task learning, due to the shared representations and.URI similarities between the two tasks. However, we may also observe overfitting or decreased performance if the VAE is not able to effectively balance the two tasks or if the tasks are too dissimilar.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Universal Framework for Neural Identity Representation from Population Activity
PROPOSAL: Integrate and compare the findings from the previous experiments, and propose a unified framework for neural identity representation from population activity. We will distill the key insights and discoveries from the individual experiments, and identify common themes and underlying principles that can inform the development of a general framework.
CONTROLS: None, this proposal serves as a summary and synthesis of the individual experiments.
COST: N/A (not requiring additional computational resources)
PREDICTION: The unified framework should provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors that influence neural identity representation, and offer guidance on how to design and develop effective neural identity representation models that can generalize across different populations, encoding schemes, and tasks.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Learning of Population-Invariant Neuron Representations
PROPOSAL: Train a variational autoencoder (VAE) on Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice from multiple brain regions, with a population-invariant loss term that encourages the VAE to capture neuron-level features that generalize across sessions and brain regions. Specifically, use a내 VA(self-Similarity) layer to compute the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the embedding distribution of a neuron and its average embedding across all other neurons in the population. The total loss function combines VAE's reconstruction loss and the self-similarity loss term.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline of multi-task learning on separate neuron classification tasks (cell type and brain region) using a single neural network architecture.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The VAE-based approach will achieve better generalization across sessions and brain regions compared to the baseline, with a consistent 5-10% improvement in classification accuracy. Challenges may arise when the number of labeled neurons is low or when the population diversity is high, leading to poor performance in those regimes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Learning with Auxiliary Populations
PROPOSAL: Modify the VAE from proposal 1 by adding a semi-supervised learning component, where the model is trained on a labeled subset of neurons (e.g. 10% of the total population) and an unlabeled subset of auxiliary populations (e.g. recordings from adjacent brain regions or different sessions). The auxiliary populations provide additional context and diversity without compromising the model's ability to capture session- and brain region-invariant features. To train the model, use a multi-task objective that combines the original VAE loss with a contrastive loss term that encourages the labeled neuron embeddings to be closer to the supervisory class labels than to the unlabeled auxiliary population embeddings.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the semi-supervised model on a random subset of neurons not included in the labeled or auxiliary populations, and compare against a baseline that trains a single-task supervised model on the labeled neurons.
COST: 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The semi-supervised model will improve classification accuracy by an additional 2-5% compared to the unsupervised baseline, especially in regions with limited labeled data, but may suffer in scenarios where the auxiliary populations are noisy or unrelated to the labeled neurons.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Learning with Auxiliary Populations
REVISION: Modify the contrastive loss term to incorporate a probabilistic perspective by assuming that the neuron labels are categorical and come from a discrete distribution. Introduce a latently encoded label (label embedding) space, where each label embedding captures the underlying distribution of the corresponding category. Train the model to generate a label embedding based on the input neuron's representation and encourage the generated label embedding to be close to the corresponding label embedding in the latently encoded space. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Universal Neuron Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We design an offline pre-training approach for Universal Neural Embedding (UNE), which learns dense vector representations of neurons from diverse Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice. UNE leverages a contrastive learning objective, contrasting the representation of a neuron with those of its nearest neighbors in feature space and with neurons from non-matching cells. The UNE model will be pre-trained on a large-scale dataset of Neuropixels recordings and then fine-tuned on neuron identity labels for cell type classification and brain region identification tasks.
CONTROLS: Our baseline will be a state-of-the-art neural activity processing model, PESN (Population-encoded spike sequence network). We will also evaluate an ablation study removing the contrastive loss term and a control experiment pre-training the model on brain region labels instead of anchor contrast.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UNE should achieve state-of-the-art performance on cell type classification and brain region identification tasks with robust zero-shot transfer across different recordings, yet we might overfit to the pre-training task and lose performance when fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the role of sub-sampling
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of sub-sampling Neuropixels recordings on the performance of the pre-trained Universal Neural Embeddings (UNE) when fine-tuned for cell type classification and brain region identification. We explore different sub-sampling ratios to assess how representative a subset of neurons and their accompanying network activity are of the full dataset. Additionally, we analyze the feature space to understand how the contrastive loss objective is being used during pre-training.
CONTROLS: We will use the same baseline and ablation study from proposal 1. We will also perform a full set analysis where we fine-tune UNE on the full dataset to compare results.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that sub-sampling will negatively impact performance when the sub-sampling ratio is too aggressive, as it leads to reduced representation capacity in the UNE. However, moderate sub-sampling may preserve performance, and we need to determine the optimal ratio for UNE.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating UNE on calcium imaging recordings
PROPOSAL: We adapt the Universal Neural Embeddings (UNE) to learn from calcium imaging recordings in mice, which capture neural activity at a different timescale than Neuropixels recordings. We evaluate the transferability of the pre-trained UNE model to this new modality by fine-tuning it on calcium imaging recordings and assessing performance on cell type classification and brain region identification tasks.
CONTROLS: We use the same baseline and ablation study from proposals 1 and 2, trained on Neuropixels data. We also fine-tune the pre-trained UNE model directly on calcium imaging data to compare results.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that UNE will perform reasonably well on calcium imaging data, demonstrating its ability to adapt to a new modality. However, we anticipate some performance degradation due to differences in the data characteristics and the need for additional fine-tuning, which might require more data and hyperparameter tuning.

PREDICTION: We anticipate that task-specific fine-tuning in the embedding space can be a powerful extension to our pre-trained Universal Neural Embeddings, enabling state-of-the-art performance on cell type classification, brain region identification and adapting well to the calcium imaging modality.

TITLE: Scalability study of UNE on Neuropixels data
PROPOSAL: We perform an extensive scalability study to understand the effect of increasing data volume and neuron count on the performance and computational requirements of the Universal Neural Embeddings (UNE) model. We record Neuropixels data from multiple experiments and evaluate how the model's performance scales with the number of neurons, electrodes, and recording sessions.

PROPOSAL: We evaluate the zero-shot transferability of the pre-trained Universal Neural Embeddings (UNE) across different Neuropixels experiments with varying cell types, brain regions, and recording conditions. By freezing the pre-trained model, we fine-tune it on a small number of labeled neurons from one experiment and test its performance on unlabeled data from a different experiment.
CONTROLS: We use the scalable UNE model architecture from proposal 5 as a baseline and compare it to a state-of-the-art transfer learning model, MAML, for cell type classification and brain region identification.
COST: 300 GPU-hours

However, performance may degrade if the target experiment has drastically different recording conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neuronal subpopulation discovery using UNE
PROPOSAL: We extend the Universal Neural Embeddings (UNE) framework to identify and cluster neuronal subpopulations with distinct characteristics, such as receptor expression profiles or anatomical locations. We employ cluster analysis on the pre-trained UNE representations and evaluate the discovered subpopulations in terms of their consistency, heterogeneity, and relation to known neuronal compartments.
CONTROLS: We use the scalable UNE model architecture from proposal 5 for clustering, and apply established techniques for feature visualization and subpopulation interpretation. Additionally, we compare our results to labels from existing cell type classification benchmarks.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the pre-trained UNE model's ability to capture rich population context, we expect to identify consistently defined subpopulations that reflect subtle differences in neural activity patterns. Some identified subpopulations might correspond to specific neuron types, while others may represent intermediate states or dynamically changing populations.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Initial Baseline Experiment for Direct FACS Based Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Train a linear regression model to predict the exact weights for the controlled activations in a linear FACS blendshape rig from a set of labeled data sampled from artist-created blendshape rigs across a variety of real-world faces.
CONTROLS: Compare against: (1) fixed weights assigned via knowledge distillation from a pre-trained network that was trained to predict blendshape activations from artist-created FACS parameterizations, and (2) the null model that predicts constant weights across all sample points and FACS parameters.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (~1 week on a single NVIDIA V100)
PREDICTION: Our baseline model will likely show good prediction capacity but fail in its ability to generalize to unseen faces due to the lack of overfitting handling, producing effective weights in around 70% of test cases but missing by a significant margin in the remaining 30%.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Neural Network Architecture for FACS-Based Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Design a deep neural network - a regressing version of a Face-XL model (Ji et al., 2020), tailored to output the weights and control signals needed for FACS blendshape rigs on any input face. Use two decoders to output a single joint-map of vertex weights, where one maps input facial landmarks to a conditional embedding space and the other maps from this embedding to vertex weights of the target FG-BSP (Fine-Grained Basic Shape Parameters) model.
CONTROLS: Compare against: (1) the baseline linear regression model (1) with this design of neural network architecture and capacity.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (~3 weeks on a single NVIDIA V100)
PREDICTION: Significant improvement over the baseline, with the network successfully capturing subtle correlations between facial features and blendshape weights, and generalizing over test cases that are quite different from the training set.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Initial Baseline Experiment for Direct FACS Based Facial Rigging
PROPOSAL: Train a lightweight variant of the previously suggested linear regression model (ordinary least squares instead of ridge regression, and a simple self-normalizing architecture), and compare it against not only the previously suggested null model but also a number of image-based baselines (proposing warp transformations given set landmarks on the input image, that have proposed keypoints moved to their locations). As previously suggested, also compare against: (1) fixed weights assigned via knowledge distillation from a pre-trained network that was trained to predict blendshape activations from artist-created FACS parameterizations.
CONTROLS: This controls for the difference in performance coming from different designs, choice of data pre-processing or machinery for training the model, and compare our self-normalizing variant in a specific simplified set of architectures.
COST: No change from 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: As before, we anticipate moderate performance from both our revised baseline model and our full network architecture, however our baseline is likely able to fairly well generalise across a wider variety of facial shapes.
